false_positives.candidate:
Salesforce refresh calls prisma without importing it

The new getClient path calls prisma.credential.update after exchanging the refresh token, but this file never imports prisma. Reaching that line throws ReferenceError: prisma is not defined and fails typecheck. getClient runs from the SalesforceCalendarService constructor, so every Salesforce create, update, or availability check throws and no connection is returned. This is not gated on credential sync, so it breaks existing Salesforce installs on deploy.

Salesforce refreshes the OAuth token on every client construction

getClient always POSTs to the Salesforce token endpoint before building the connection, with no check that the stored access token is still valid. Availability and booking construct SalesforceCalendarService often, so each call adds a token round trip and consumes Salesforce OAuth quota. Previously the connection was created from the stored token and jsforce refreshed only when Salesforce rejected it. This extra call is not limited to credential sync, so it regresses every Salesforce user, and a token-endpoint failure now breaks operations that still had a valid access token.

Outbound credential sync request is unauthenticated

The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only calcomUserId and appSlug. It does not send CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET, a signature, or an Authorization header, and it does not check response.ok. The inbound webhook that writes credentials requires the shared secret, but the call that returns live access tokens does not prove it came from this Cal.com instance. An endpoint implemented to match this client cannot tell Cal.com from any other caller, so anyone who can reach that URL can request access tokens for arbitrary user ids and app slugs.

Credential webhook can insert duplicate rows

The handler uses findFirst and then updates or creates, with no transaction, lock, or unique constraint on (userId, appId). userId and type are not unique on Credential (other OAuth callbacks already special-case duplicates). Two deliveries for the same user and app, including a retry, can both see no row and both insert. findFirst has no orderBy, so a later sync updates an arbitrary duplicate while calendar code that also uses findFirst can keep the stale key. The user ends up with two credentials and the integration may keep using outdated tokens.

Credential sync does not clear the invalid flag

The update path writes only key and does not set invalid to false. Google, Webex, and Zoom set invalid after invalid_grant and then skip that credential. If a self-hoster pushes a fresh key for that user, this endpoint still returns 200, but Cal.com keeps ignoring the row, so the integration stays disconnected until the flag is cleared or the user reinstalls the app.

Zoom sync slug is "zoomvideo" but credentials are stored as "zoom"

refreshOAuthTokens is called with appSlug "zoomvideo", but the Zoom callback creates the credential with appId "zoom", and the new webhook stores appId from the app metadata slug, which is "zoom" for this app. The parent platform is the source of truth keyed by slug. A sync or refresh using one of these strings will not find the credential written under the other, so Zoom tokens will not update, or a second credential will be created under the wrong slug and never used by the video adapter.

Lark deletes the credential before sync refresh can run

refreshAccessToken still deletes the credential and throws when the local refresh token is missing or refresh_expires_date has passed, and that check runs before refreshOAuthTokens. With credential sync enabled, the parent app holds the real tokens and the local refresh token may be expired or absent, which is exactly when the sync endpoint should be called. Instead the row is deleted, the sync URL is never hit, and the user must reconnect Lark. The sync branch has to run before this destructive local-token check.

No tests for credential sync or shared OAuth refresh

This PR changes token refresh for Google, Office 365, Zoom, HubSpot, Lark, Webex, Zoho, and Salesforce and adds a webhook that writes credential rows, but it adds no tests. The PR checklist says tests were not added and were not run. The sync-disabled path needs a test that a provider response without refresh_token does not overwrite the stored refresh token and that credential.key is the token object, not a Zod safeParse wrapper. The sync-enabled path needs tests that the outbound request is authenticated, sends the user id rather than the credential id, and that each adapter can read the response. Without that, the credential corruption in parseRefreshTokenResponse and Google CalendarService is not caught before deploy.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation is never awaited, so the cancelled flag can be dropped

deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are fired inside forEach and never awaited, then the handler awaits unrelated deletes and returns "Booking successfully cancelled." The email fix only persists if WorkflowReminder.cancelled is updated, and SMS cancellation only happens inside that discarded promise. The same un-awaited pattern is in handleNewBooking.ts around line 966, packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx around line 488, and packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx around lines 212, 376, 519, and 574. On serverless the isolate can freeze when the response is sent, so the update never commits and the reminder is still delivered. The try/catch around the reschedule forEach does not help: forEach does not await, and both helpers swallow their own errors. This replaces an awaited prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany. Callers must await every cancellation (Promise.all or for-of) before returning or deleting parent rows.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the asynchronous functions `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are called inside `forEach` loops without being awaited across booking and workflow handlers, which can cause reminder cancellations to fail or not complete reliably.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete reintroduces the SendGrid 100-cap and drops the retry record

When immediateDelete is true the helper POSTs a SendGrid batch cancel and returns without setting cancelled and without deleting the WorkflowReminder. Callers pass true for reschedules (handleNewBooking.ts:968) and for workflow/step deletion (workflows.tsx:214 and workflows.tsx:521). That immediate POST is the usage this PR is trying to stop: cancelled batches stay in SendGrid scheduled_sends until the original send time, and the cap is 100 pending cancellations. Reschedules and workflow deletes fill that cap, later cancels fail, and those emails are still sent. Failures are caught inside the helper, so the caller continues as if cancellation worked. On reschedule the booking is kept, the row is left with cancelled unset, and the cron only cancels cancelled=true rows, so it will not retry. On workflow and step deletion the POST is not awaited and the following delete cascade-removes the reminder (WorkflowStep/Workflow onDelete: Cascade). If the POST has not finished or failed because of the cap, the batch id is gone and the cron cannot retry, so the email is sent. Far-future sends should only set cancelled and keep the row. A workflow or step must not cascade the reminder away until SendGrid cancel has succeeded.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: when `immediateDelete` is true, the function cancels the SendGrid batch and returns without deleting the `WorkflowReminder` record or setting `cancelled` in the database. The candidate also provides additional context about SendGrid limits and retry mechanics, which expands upon the same underlying flaw.

false_positives.candidate:
All email cancels are deferred, so reminders due before the next cron are still sent

For any reminder that already has a referenceId, cancellation only sets cancelled=true and never calls SendGrid, no matter how soon scheduledDate is. The only follow-up is the scheduleEmailReminders cron (PR: every 15 minutes), which cancels batches whose scheduledDate is within the next hour. SendGrid will not cancel a scheduled send less than 10 minutes before sendAt. If the booking is cancelled after the last cron run that is still more than 10 minutes before send time, the next run either happens after scheduledDate — and that job first deletes every EMAIL reminder with scheduledDate <= now, so cancel is never attempted — or SendGrid rejects the late cancel. The reminder is delivered. This is the common case of cancelling shortly before a reminder. Deferral also does not protect the 100-cap for sends already inside the one-hour window, because those cancellations would be pending for under an hour either way. Reminders already inside that window should be cancelled immediately; only later sends should be flagged for the cron.

Past-due reminders are deleted before SendGrid cancellation is attempted

The cron starts by deleting every EMAIL WorkflowReminder with scheduledDate <= now, including rows with cancelled=true, and only then loads reminders to cancel (lines 44-51). The row is the only copy of the SendGrid batch id. If an earlier run did not cancel that batch (downtime, a thrown cancel aborting the loop, or the booking being cancelled after the last pre-send run), SendGrid still has the scheduled mail and this delete makes a later cancel impossible. Past-due cleanup must not remove cancelled rows until a SendGrid cancel has been attempted and the outcome recorded. As written, any missed window permanently fails the fix.

One SendGrid cancel failure aborts the rest and skips DB cleanup

remindersToCancel is handled in a single try/catch. Each POST is awaited in order, and the prisma deletes are only executed after every request succeeds. Any rejection — the 100 pending-cancellation cap, SendGrid refusing a cancel inside its 10-minute cutoff, a null referenceId, or a network error — jumps to the catch, which only logs, then the handler goes on to schedule new mail. Later reminders in that run are not cancelled. Rows whose POST already succeeded are not deleted, so the next run must redo them. A row that fails every time stays in the result set until its scheduledDate passes and the earlier deleteMany removes it, and each run that hits it aborts the rest of the batch, so those other cancelled reminders are sent. The query also does not require method EMAIL or a non-null referenceId, so one bad row is enough to fail the POST. Handle each reminder independently, skip rows without a batch id, and delete a row only after its own cancel succeeds.

Paid booking cancellation returns before workflow reminders are cancelled

If the booking is paid, this branch refunds, sets status to REJECTED, and returns "Booking successfully cancelled." before the reminder block at line 484. That block is the only place this handler marks email reminders cancelled or deletes SMS reminders. The earlier return null when the payment app is missing (around line 437) skips it too. Paid event types can still have workflows, and bookingToDelete already loads workflowReminders, but they are ignored on this path. A cancelled paid booking therefore keeps its scheduled emails and SMS. If the reminder was not yet handed to SendGrid, the cron's unscheduled query does not check booking status and will schedule and send it; if it was already scheduled, the cron only cancels rows with cancelled=true, which was never set. Reminder cancellation has to run on this path before returning.

Every workflow save recreates reminders while old SendGrid batches stay live

An existing step is treated as edited when JSON.stringify(oldStep) !== JSON.stringify(newStep). oldStep is a Prisma WorkflowStep and always includes numberVerificationPending; newStep is the zod input and has senderName instead, so the comparison is always true even when nothing changed. The branch used to delete the WorkflowReminder row; that deleteMany was removed. It now only calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder (line 576), which sets cancelled and leaves the SendGrid scheduled send in place, and that call is not awaited. The same request then scheduleEmailReminder's a new batch for every future booking of that step. Every workflow save therefore leaves the previous batches live until the cron's one-hour window and adds another set. Near-term reminders can be delivered twice. All superseded batches become pending cancellations in the same hour, which can exceed SendGrid's 100-cap and cause the cron cancel loop to fail. Compare the actual editable fields, and do not create the replacement send until the previous batch is flagged or cancelled.

No tests for deferred cancel or the cron SendGrid cancellation loop

The PR replaces SendGrid cancellation and adds a cron path, but no test covers deleteScheduledEmailReminder, the cancelled flag, reschedule/workflow-delete behavior, or the scheduleEmailReminders cancellation loop. The previous fix used the wrong SendGrid endpoint and failed in production once 100 pending cancellations accumulated. Without a test that a far-future cancel only sets cancelled, that an imminent cancel actually stops the batch, and that one failed POST does not skip the remaining rows, the same production failure can regress unnoticed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blacklist and duplicate checks are case-sensitive

BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS values are lowercased but not trimmed, and the submitted address is not trimmed or lowercased before includes(). A blocked address with different casing, or a blacklist entry with a leading space after the comma, is stored and emailed. Duplicate detection uses case-sensitive equality, so A@x.com and a@x.com both become Attendee rows, and the organizer's own email is not excluded. The read of existing attendees is also outside a transaction, so two parallel requests can both pass the filter and insert the same guest. Normalize both sides with trim and lowercase, trim blacklist entries, and do not add the organizer as an attendee. Mixed requests currently drop blocked or duplicate addresses silently and still return success.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin/owner check can never succeed

isTeamAdminOrOwner is computed with && between isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner. Membership role is a single value, so a user is never both ADMIN and OWNER, and the && short-circuits. If isTeamAdmin matches only ADMIN, the check is always false; if it also treats OWNER as admin, only owners pass and admins still fail. Either way team admins cannot add guests unless they are also the booking organizer or an attendee, which contradicts the variable name and the permission gate. The bookings UI still shows Additional guests on confirmed rows, so those users hit FORBIDDEN. Use ||, and skip the lookup when eventType.teamId is null instead of querying team id 0.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.

sendAddGuestsEmails is called with the raw guests input, not uniqueGuests, the addresses actually inserted. In that helper, any attendee whose email is in the list receives AttendeeScheduledEmail (a full new-booking confirmation with cancel and reschedule links) instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail. If the request includes someone already on the booking plus a new guest, the existing person is not inserted again but still gets a fresh scheduled email and does not get the guests-added notice. The includes() check is also case-sensitive. Pass the normalized list of addresses that were actually added.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: `sendAddGuestsEmails` is passed the raw input `guests` array (referred to as `newGuests` inside the function) instead of the filtered list of actually added guests, which causes the `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` check to wrongly classify existing attendees as new guests when deciding between sending `AttendeeScheduledEmail` vs `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Add-guest emails ignore disabled standard emails

sendAddGuestsEmails always emails the organizer and every attendee. Other helpers in this file (sendScheduledEmails, sendLocationChangeEmails, sendCancelledEmails, and the rest) skip host or attendee mail when event-type metadata disables standard emails. This helper has no such check, and addGuestsHandler never passes eventType.metadata. Organizers who turned those emails off still get guest-added mail and full AttendeeScheduledEmail messages, including ICS and meeting links, when guests are added. Pass the metadata through and honor the same disable flags.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the `sendAddGuestsEmails` function fails to check the event-type metadata for flags that disable standard emails (`disableStandardEmails`), causing emails to be sent to hosts and attendees even when disabled.

false_positives.candidate:
Calendar update uses the caller's credentials

EventManager is built from the signed-in user and getUsersCredentials(ctx.user). Calendar BookingReferences are tied to the organizer's credential id (and other hosts' credentials on collective events), not the caller's. The query already loads booking.user with credentials and destinationCalendar and never uses that user. When an attendee adds guests, the host calendar event is not updated. On collective events, other hosts' calendar copies cannot be updated either because only one user's credentials are supplied. Load decrypted credentials for the booking organizer (getUsersCredentials, not the raw Prisma credential rows) and include collective hosts.

Any attendee can invite unlimited guests on any booking

Authorization only checks organizer, attendee, or the broken team-admin flag. booking.status, end time, and list size are never validated, and ZAddGuestsInputSchema is an unbounded email array. Any logged-in attendee can therefore add as many addresses as they want to a cancelled, rejected, unconfirmed, or past booking. Each new address is sent AttendeeScheduledEmail, and the mailer hardcodes ICS status CONFIRMED. videoCallData (join URL and meeting password) is copied onto the event whenever a video reference exists, so those invites disclose meeting access for events that are not accepted upcoming meetings, and a participant can send unlimited calendar mail through the platform. Restrict this to accepted future bookings and cap the guest list.

Seated events are not capacity-checked

Guests are inserted as Attendee rows with no comparison to eventType.seatsPerTimeSlot, which is only copied onto the calendar payload later. If occupancy is the attendee count, this overbooks the slot and can block real bookers. If occupancy is BookingSeat / seatsReferences, these guests become attendees with no seat, so seat counts, the seats UI, and cancel/reschedule links diverge from the attendee list. seatsShowAttendees is also ignored: sendAddGuestsEmails and the ICS include every attendee, leaking participant emails on events configured to hide them. Enforce remaining capacity before insert, or reject add-guests for seated events, and honor seatsShowAttendees when emailing.

Guests stay saved when calendar or email updates fail

prisma.booking.update commits the new Attendee rows before translation loading, updateCalendarAttendees, and sendAddGuestsEmails. The calendar call is outside the try/catch, so a thrown calendar or translation error returns 500 after the insert. A retry then filters those addresses out as already present and throws emails_must_be_unique_valid, so the calendar update and invite emails are never retried and the user is told the addresses are invalid. Email failures are caught, logged as a static string with the error discarded, and the handler still returns success, so the dialog toasts Guests added when nobody was notified. Roll back or make the side effects retryable, and do not report success when notification failed.

New guests are stored with a blank name

Every newly inserted guest is saved with name set to an empty string. Scheduled and add-guest mail payloads address the recipient as `${attendee.name} <${attendee.email}>`, so new guests, who are sent AttendeeScheduledEmail, get a blank display name (` <email>`). The same empty name is sent in the calendar attendee update. Use the email address, or its local part, when no name was collected.

Collective co-hosts are never notified

The CalendarEvent built for notifications never sets team or team.members, even though eventType is already loaded. sendAddGuestsEmails only emails extra hosts when calendarEvent.team.members is present, so that loop never runs. On a collective event, only booking.user receives OrganizerAddGuestsEmail; the other hosts are not told that guests were added. Load the event-type hosts and set calEvent.team the same way other booking mail flows do.

Add-guests is offered on past bookings

The new additional-guests action is added to editBookingActions, which is included in bookedActions. bookedActions is not limited to upcoming meetings: past confirmed bookings and past pending bookings also render TableActions with that list. Using it still inserts attendees and sends AttendeeScheduledEmail plus an ICS REQUEST for a time that already passed. Only show this action for accepted upcoming bookings, and enforce the same rule in addGuestsHandler.

No tests for addGuests authorization or failure paths

The new mutation ships with no unit or integration tests. The inverted team-admin condition, access to cancelled or past bookings, seated overbooking, blacklist casing, and a calendar or email failure after the attendee insert would not be caught in CI. Cover organizer, team admin, team owner, attendee, and stranger; non-accepted bookings; seat capacity; and a side-effect failure after insert.

true_positives.golden_comment: Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code comparison is case-sensitive and unnormalized

Codes are generated as lowercase hex (crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex") in setup.ts) and login compares them with indexOf after only stripping "-". The same check is in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts at the backupCode.replaceAll call. There is no toLowerCase() or trim, and spaces are left in place. The recovery input in apps/web/components/auth/BackupCode.tsx uses placeholder "XXXXX-XXXXX" and does not set autoCapitalize="none", so mobile keyboards and anyone following the placeholder submit uppercase hex. Those attempts always fail as an incorrect backup code, which blocks the recovery path when the authenticator is already lost. Normalize by trimming, removing dashes and spaces, and lowercasing on the server, and stop advertising uppercase in the field.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: backup code validation uses a case-sensitive `indexOf()` comparison without normalizing/lowercasing the input, causing validation to fail if the user enters uppercase hex characters.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
One-time backup codes are consumed with a lost update

Redeeming a backup code decrypts the stored list, finds a match, sets that slot to null, and writes the whole blob back with a plain user.update keyed only by id. There is no transaction, row lock, or compare-and-swap on the previous ciphertext. Two overlapping logins can both read the same list and both succeed: the same code opens two sessions, and if the requests use two different codes the later write restores the code the earlier request consumed. The promise that each code works exactly once is therefore not enforced. Consume the code with a conditional update (or SELECT FOR UPDATE) that fails if backupCodes changed, and only then issue the session.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same race condition (TOCTOU / lost update) when redeeming backup codes: decrypting, modifying in memory, and writing back without locking or conditional updates allows concurrent requests to reuse the same backup code.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup-code login skips the password when totpCode is set

Password verification runs only when `user.password` is set and `credentials.totpCode` is empty (the check around line 121). The new backup-code branch then logs the user in if the backup code matches and never validates `totpCode`. A request with the victim's email, any non-empty totpCode (for example "000000"), and a valid backup code therefore skips the password entirely, consumes that code, and creates a session. Backup codes are supposed to replace the authenticator only; the login UI still sends the password and clears totpCode, but the credentials callback must not trust the client to omit totpCode. Anyone who obtains a backup code (the downloaded cal-backup-codes.txt, a screenshot, a clipboard history) can take over the account without the password. Verify the password inside this branch whenever the user has one, and do not treat an unchecked totpCode as proof the password was already accepted.

Closing the codes dialog does not finish 2FA setup

On a successful enable response the modal only moves to DisplayBackupCodes and no longer calls onEnable(). onEnable() runs solely from the footer Close button. Escape, the overlay, and the dialog's default close control go through onOpenChange and do not notify the parent, so the settings switch stays off while twoFactorEnabled is already true on the server. Now the calendar path awaits getCalendar before deleteEvent, and deleteMeeting (videoClient.ts) awaits getVideoAdapters before calling the provider, and nothing awaits either promise. The old event can remain on the external calendar and the video meeting can stay up; on serverless the runtime often freezes that work after the handler returns, so the cleanup never runs. DogStatsD/statsd tag lists are comma-separated, so a comma inside the value is parsed as extra tags and the timer is dropped or recorded as a truncated series such as shard:0. Rebalances also mint a new series per assignment, which is unbounded cardinality. Emit one shard id per point (or omit the tag when shards are grouped) and use the same key on all three metrics.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op, then after setting fac._flusher.current_drift calls time.sleep(0.1) to let the flusher thread observe the new clock. That call is the patched no-op, so it does not wait, and the extra step.poll() does not flush either: SpanFlusher.poll only forwards to the committer while flushing runs on the background thread. step.join() then sets the shared stopped flag before it waits for the thread. If the thread has not yet read the updated drift, it sees stopped and exits without producing, and (msg,) = messages fails. The race is intermittent and worse under CI load. Wait with a sleep that was bound before the patch, or poll messages until the payload appears, using a real timeout.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hung spawn flushers are never killed, so restarts overlap

Workers are created with multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process, i.e. SpawnProcess. That class subclasses multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess, not multiprocessing.Process, so isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is always false for real flusher processes. The new guard therefore never calls kill() in _ensure_processes_alive, and the same check in join() never calls terminate(). Previously kill() was unconditional, so this is a regression on the default single-process path as well as the multi-process path. A hung worker is left running, the restart counter is incremented, and _create_process_for_shards overwrites self.processes and drops the only reference the strategy keeps. The orphan keeps calling flush_segments/produce/done_flush_segments on the same shards as the replacement, which can duplicate segments on the buffered-segments topic or delete Redis state the other worker is still producing. The replacement also resets process_healthy_since, so once it looks healthy the parent stops retrying and the orphan runs until the consumer process exits. join() likewise cannot SIGTERM a worker blocked in Redis or Kafka that never observes the stopped flag. Thread-mode restarts (produce_to_pipe) leak the same way because nothing stops the previous thread. Even after the type check is fixed (use BaseProcess, or skip only threading.Thread), kill() is asynchronous and the replacement is started immediately with no join; the old worker must be reaped before a new one is started.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Timed join returns while flusher processes are still running

join() sets a deadline, spends the full timeout in next_step.join(timeout), then walks flusher workers. If the deadline is already exhausted it breaks immediately; if it expires mid-loop the break skips every remaining worker. Those workers are neither waited on nor terminated. close() intentionally does not stop flushers (to avoid a Redis memory spike at rebalance start), so join() is the only shutdown barrier. A worker blocked in flush_segments or Kafka produce will not see stopped until that call returns, and after the break nothing signals it. Kafka rebalance then builds a new SpanFlusher for the same shards — in this process or another — while the old workers are still flushing, so both produce the same segments and race on Redis flush markers. The previous single-process join always fell through to terminate() after the wait; the early break is a regression. On the way out of join(), every worker that is still alive must be killed and joined, including when the timeout is already spent.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: breaking out of the flusher shutdown loop when the deadline expires skips termination of remaining workers, potentially leaving them running after shutdown. Error and breadcrumb timestamps are not on the same scale

gen_request_data interleaves errors and breadcrumbs with error["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0). Replay segment events are raw rrweb records whose timestamp is epoch milliseconds. fetch_error_details copies the nodestore event timestamp, which is epoch seconds (or sometimes an ISO string). Seconds are always less than millisecond breadcrumbs, so every error is emitted before the first breadcrumb and the summary chronology is wrong for real replays. An ISO-string timestamp raises TypeError on < or sort, and that exception is outside fetch_error_details's try/except, so the summarize request 500s. The new tests hide this by writing segment JSON with now.timestamp() seconds. Normalize both sides to the same numeric unit before comparing.

Error ids are queried with the page stats window, not the replay

Error context now depends on query_replay_instance(start=filter_params["start"], end=filter_params["end"]) from ProjectEndpoint.get_filter_params. The replay AI tab (static/app/views/replays/detail/ai/index.tsx) calls this endpoint with no start, end, or statsPeriod. The lookup therefore uses the generic project default stats window rather than the replay's own start/end. Replays outside that window return no row, error_ids stays empty, and the summary is produced without error context with no error to the user. Query the replay by id over its retention window, or pass the replay bounds from the client.

Hidden span attributes are only removed while searching

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES (is_segment, project_id, received) is applied only inside the searchQuery branch. When the search box is empty the code returns sortAttributes(attributes) unchanged, so those internal fields stay visible. Once the user types a query that would match them, they disappear. If the intent is to hide them, filter them out before the search check; otherwise search results disagree with the full list.

Feedback list is clipped after the summary is inserted

The list grid cell used to be a FluidHeight Container (height 100% of the stretched grid area). It is now SummaryListContainer, a column flex with no min-height: 0 or overflow handling, containing FeedbackSummary plus that same height-100% Container. The list's 100% height is the full cell, then the summary and gap are added on top, so the column overflows the grid row. Background and LayoutGrid both set overflow: hidden, so the bottom of the feedback list is clipped and no longer lines up with the details pane. Give the list container flex: 1 and min-height: 0 (and overflow: hidden) so it fills only the space under the summary.

Attribute-key hook returns undefined after a failed fetch

useTraceItemAttributeKeys used to always reduce the API payload to a TagCollection (empty object if data was missing) and return that once loading finished. It now returns useQuery's data directly: attributes is previous while isFetching, otherwise data. On error, isFetching is false and data is undefined, and there is no ?? {}. Explore callers that wait for !isLoading and then spread or Object.keys the result will throw, blanking the search builder, instead of seeing an empty tag set. Return data ?? {} (and keep the previous value only while refetching).

Feedback summary ignores the environment page filter

useFeedbackSummary reads usePageFilters().selection and sends normalized datetime plus project, but not selection.environments. The feedback list on the same page is scoped by the environment page filter. With an environment selected, the summary is computed from every environment in the projects and date range, so it can describe feedback the list is not showing. Pass environment (and any other page filters the summary API supports) in the query.

60s deadline is too short for a 100-identity auth refresh

check_auth_identities now has processing_deadline_duration=60 while it still loops up to chunk_size (default 100) identities, each doing an org-membership RPC and provider.refresh_identity HTTP call. 100 sequential IdP calls routinely exceed 60s, so the taskworker kills the task mid-batch. check_auth already sets last_synced=now on those ids before enqueueing this task, and they are not selected again until the next ~24h window (AUTH_CHECK_INTERVAL). Identities not yet refreshed are skipped for a day, so SSO invalidation is delayed. Raise the deadline to match the chunk, or shrink the chunk to what 60s can finish.

Issue titles are interpolated into markdown links unsanitized

MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE is "* ‼️ [**{title}**]({url}){environment}\n" and _truncate_title only slices to 50 characters. Issue titles come from user-influenced error messages. A title containing ] or ) breaks out of the link, for example [**click here](https://evil.example)**](real-url), and is posted to GitHub/GitLab. Truncation does not stop that. Escape markdown metacharacters in the title (and backticks in the environment name) before formatting.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Access-token ID matcher checks the wrong characters and inverts the match

isAccessTokenId is now what expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken, and expectAuthReqIdToToken use for Details.TOKEN_ID. After splitting on ':', it treats items[0].substring(3, 5) as the grant shortcut and returns false (no match) when that slice equals the expected shortcut. Both parts are wrong. The wire format is 2-char session type, 2-char token type, 2-char grant type, so the grant is substring(4, 6): for onrtac the grant is ac, while substring(3, 5) is ta (last char of token type 'rt'/'lt' plus the first grant char). The equality test is also inverted, so a real match is rejected. For every built-in grant, substring(3, 5) is 't' plus the grant's first character, which is never the grant shortcut, so the check never fires and the matcher accepts any six-char prefix plus a UUID. These new assertions will not fail if authorization-code, refresh, device, or CIBA access tokens are encoded with the wrong grant (including the 'na' fallback). A prefix shorter than 5 characters throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of a failed assertion. The check should require a prefix of at least 6 characters and substring(4, 6) equal to the expected shortcut.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies both aspects of the golden issue: the grant shortcut should use substring(4, 6), and equality with the expected shortcut should indicate a match rather than return false, alongside UUID validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grant shortcuts are not validated as 2-character unique codes

Access-token ids are a fixed 6-character prefix (session type, token type, grant shortcut, 2 characters each) plus ':' plus the raw id. The decoder rejects any other prefix length. postInit stores each grant shortcut with no check that it is non-null, exactly 2 characters, free of ':', or unique beyond a map-size comparison. OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut's javadoc says shortcuts are 'usually like 3-letters', which cannot be represented in this format. A custom grant that follows that javadoc still passes the size check, and encodeTokenId will issue ids such as onrtabc:<uuid>. Decoding those ids throws IllegalArgumentException, so the context this feature exists to recover is unreadable. The hot-deploy refresh in getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut (puts around lines 113 and 131) also overwrites grantsByShortcuts without re-checking length or uniqueness. Two grants that share a shortcut leave one decode mapping, so previously issued tokens of the overwritten grant are reported as the other grant type. Registration should reject anything other than a unique 2-character shortcut, and the javadoc must match that contract.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same Javadoc mismatch: it describes shortcuts as usually three letters despite actual usage requiring two characters, and recommends correcting the documentation. Its additional validation concerns do not negate that match.

false_positives.candidate:
New getShortcut() method has no default and aborts server startup

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is the extension point for custom grant types, and getShortcut() was added with no default implementation. DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit walks every OAuth2GrantType factory and calls getShortcut() unconditionally. A custom grant JAR compiled against the previous interface does not have that method, so the call throws AbstractMethodError during provider startup and Keycloak fails to boot. A recompiled factory that returns null also aborts startup, because the shortcut is inserted into a ConcurrentHashMap, which rejects null keys. A default method is required so existing providers keep the server up, and postInit must reject invalid shortcuts with an explicit error instead of an NPE or AbstractMethodError.

Decoder throws on unknown prefixes instead of falling back like legacy ids

getTokenContextFromTokenId returns an UNKNOWN session type, token type, and grant when the jti has no ':'. If the id contains ':' but the prefix is not exactly 6 characters, or any 2-character slice is missing from the in-memory maps, it throws IllegalArgumentException. The length error says the token id 'Expected length of 6', but the check is only on the prefix before the colon, so the message is wrong and will mislead operators. Unknown shortcuts are a normal compatibility case, not corruption: feature-gated grants are absent from the maps when that feature is disabled or not deployed on this node (CIBA 'ci', device 'dg', token-exchange 'te', pre-authorized code 'pc'), and another Keycloak version can mint shortcuts this node does not know. Introspection or session lookup that uses this method, which is the stated purpose of the encoding, will then fail a still-valid access token instead of falling back to the old online-then-offline lookup. Unsupported prefixes should return an UNKNOWN context, the same as colon-less legacy ids.

Non-standard token exchange issues access tokens with unknown grant

The encoded grant type is whatever was stored on the client-session attribute Constants.GRANT_TYPE. If that attribute is missing, DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider records 'na' (unknown). Token exchange does not go through OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse, which is why this provider had to set the attribute itself before generateAccessToken(). Only StandardTokenExchangeProvider.exchangeClientToOIDCClient was updated. TokenExchangeGrantTypeFactory still turns on legacy TOKEN_EXCHANGE, TOKEN_EXCHANGE_FEDERATED_V2, and TOKEN_EXCHANGE_SUBJECT_IMPERSONATION_V2, and those providers are not in this change. StandardTokenExchangeProvider rejects requested_subject, so impersonation cannot be this method. Those other flows still call TokenManager to mint access tokens, so their jti grant shortcut is 'na' rather than 'te'. Follow-up token-exchange logic that branches on the encoded grant (the #37117 case described in the PR) will not recognize them. The new AssertEvents matcher does not actually verify the grant shortcut, so CI will not catch this.

Replacing form params leaves the cached grant type stale

grantType is captured once in the Context constructor from formParams.getFirst(grant_type) and is what OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse writes into the client session before the access token id is encoded. setFormParams replaces formParams but does not recompute grantType, so getGrantType() can disagree with the params the grant then processes. A caller that uses the existing setter to change the request after construction will encode the original grant type into the access-token id. The constructor also now dereferences formParams, so a null map NPEs, which the previous constructor accepted. This change also removes the public Context(Context) copy constructor, so extensions that cloned a context that way no longer compile and have no other way to rebuild grantType.

createRecoveryCodesCredential treats a true result from user.credentialManager().updateCredential as done and returns without deleting recovery-authn-codes credentials already stored in Keycloak's local database. The local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential path is skipped in that branch, and nothing else removes those rows. Federated users who already had recovery codes locally (the only option before their user-storage provider accepted this type, or if another API wrote them locally) and then regenerate will keep the old set. UserCredentialManager.isValid accepts a code if any supporting CredentialInputValidator accepts it, and the local recovery-code provider validates local credentials independently of user storage, so the retired codes still authenticate after rotation. RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential also prefers the federated credential, so the login form can show the new code number while the old codes still work. The same gap exists in the other direction: if updateCredential returns false but user storage already holds codes, the fallback local create adds a second valid set and does not disable the user-storage one. After a successful user-storage write the helper must remove existing local recovery-authn-codes credentials, and when falling back to local storage it must disable the user-storage credential, so only one set remains valid.

false_positives.candidate:
Default update-strategy tests never enable rolling-updates

createInitialDeployment returns immediately when the update strategy is null, and the new code that sets spec.features.enabled to rolling-updates runs only for a non-null strategy. The parameterized image-change and cache-max-count tests call this helper with both null (the default strategy) and Recreate. The operator guide in this PR says that while the feature is preview it must be enabled or the operator fails, including for the default strategy that still decides rolling vs recreate on image changes. The default-strategy cases therefore never put rolling-updates on the Keycloak CR, which is the configuration users are told to set. Those tests either fail when the compatibility command rejects a feature-disabled server, or they pass only because operator/scripts/Dockerfile-custom-image now bakes the feature into the test image and never cover the documented CR path. Enable the feature for every deployment this helper builds, before the null return. setEnabledFeatures(List.of(...)) also replaces any features already on the CR instead of appending rolling-updates, so a deployment that already enables features loses them in the Recreate cases.

Exit code 4 changed meaning from recreate to feature-disabled

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE was 4 and is now 3, and 4 is reused as FEATURE_DISABLED. The update-compatibility check exit code is the public contract the guide tells automation to branch on. After this change an incompatible deployment exits 3 instead of 4, and exit 4 means the preview feature is off and no compatibility decision was made. Callers that observed the previous implementation (exit 4 = shut the deployment down and recreate) will treat a disabled feature as recreate-required, and will not treat a real incompatibility (now exit 3) as recreate-required, which can allow a rolling update the tool rejected or cause a full shutdown when the user only needed to enable the feature. The guide already listed 3 for recreate before this PR, so the old constant disagreed with the guide; if that text is the shipped contract, aligning the constant is right, but nothing in this PR updates operator production code that may still compare the job status to a literal 4. UpdateCommandDistTest does not assert either code, so CI will not catch a regression to the old value.

New and renumbered compatibility exit codes are not asserted

The distribution tests never check the exit codes this PR defines. testFeatureNotEnabled only asserts that stderr contains the disabled-feature message, and it only launches the metadata subcommand; it does not assert exit code 4, and there is no equivalent case for check. testWrongVersions only asserts the incompatibility error text after RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE moved from 4 to 3, so a build that still exits 4 (now the feature-disabled code) would still pass. The guide tells automation to branch on these codes (0 rolling, 3 recreate, 4 feature disabled). Assert the process exit code for both subcommands when rolling-updates is off, and assert exit code 3 when the stored versions are incompatible.

Documented --features flag replaces other enabled features

The updatecompatibility doc macro now renders every example as bin/kc.sh update-compatibility <args> --features=rolling-updates. Keycloak gives CLI arguments precedence over KC_FEATURES and keycloak.conf, and features is a single list-valued option, not a set merged across sources. Copying the documented command therefore replaces any other explicitly enabled features with only rolling-updates. The same guide says every option from the real deployment must be present and that omitting options produces an incorrect rolling-versus-recreate outcome. The examples should tell users to add rolling-updates to their existing enabled-feature list rather than hard-coding a replacement --features value.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
V2 client grants are not removed when the client is deleted

Per-client FGAP resources are named with the client id and are not foreign-keyed to the client, so deleting the client does not cascade them. The only hook added here is the ClientRemovedEvent listener, and the new feature gate skips that hook unless ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is enabled. In the V2-only setup this work targets, client deletion leaves the admin-permissions resource and its scope permissions in place. Listings keep a grant for a client that no longer exists, and getResourceName returns null for it. setPermissionsEnabled cannot be used to clean this up because the V2 implementation throws.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same incorrect V1 feature gate on the removal-event cleanup listener, causing orphaned permissions when only V2 is enabled. It focuses on client deletion, a specific instance of the broader role/client/group cleanup bug described in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
All-clients permission is returned as the id Clients

getClientsWithPermission adds resource.getName() for every Clients-typed resource whose evaluation grants the scope. The schema resource created for "all clients" is named Clients and has that type, so a type-level grant puts the literal string Clients into the set. That is not a client UUID. Callers that keep clients where granted.contains(client.getId()) will not treat the grant as access to every client, and nothing expands the type resource into real client ids. There is no global canMapRoles() to compensate, so an all-clients map-roles or view permission does not show those clients in filters that rely on this method.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that getClientsWithPermission iterates Clients-typed resources and returns the type-level resource name "Clients" rather than actual client IDs. Although the candidate describes filtering failures instead of the golden comment's null-client lookup failure, the underlying resource-selection and identifier bug is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Null all-clients resource NPEs permission checks

If no per-client resource exists, hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) loads the type resource with getResourceTypeResource and immediately calls PolicyStore.findByResource(server, resource). getResourceTypeResource returns null when the Clients resource was never created, was deleted, or the schema is not supported for that server (admin permissions disabled while the admin-permissions client pointer remains). findByResource dereferences the resource, so the call throws NullPointerException. The no-argument hasPermission null-checks its lookup; this overload does not. View, manage, configure, and map-roles checks that reach this fallback then 500 instead of denying, for any caller who did not already pass an admin-role short-circuit.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing null check in ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission: getResourceTypeResource can return null, which is then passed to findByResource and causes a NullPointerException.

false_positives.candidate:
Role-mapping checks drop manage-clients and master admins

canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission. They never short-circuit on root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS), unlike canManage(ClientModel). hasPermission then returns false immediately when the caller is not in the same realm. ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 installs MgmtPermissionsV2 for every realm, so this replaces the V1 evaluator: realm admins with manage-clients, and master-realm admins, can no longer map client roles, add composites, or map client-scope roles unless a fine-grained permission also grants it. V1 kept that role check inside its permission helper before any same-realm test. The new tests only use myadmin with no admin role, so they do not catch the regression. map-roles-client-scope has no test at all.

Existing admin-permissions clients never get the Clients schema

init returns as soon as realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null, and nothing in this change syncs an already created resource server. The Clients resource and the new scopes configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite are only inserted when that client is first created. Realms that already enabled fine-grained admin permissions for Users keep the old server: the Clients resource is missing and getScope fails with "Scope [configure] does not exist" (and the same for the other new scope names) when a client permission is created. Evaluation then falls through to a null type resource and can 500. Only freshly initialized realms work.

Client deletion throws when both FGAP features are enabled

The removal listener is gated on ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ, but AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, even if the V1 feature is also on. ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled always throws UnsupportedOperationException. With both features enabled, ClientRemovedEvent calls that method and the exception propagates from the provider listener, failing or rolling back client deletion. Role and group removal still use the V1 evaluators, so only clients are broken. The listener must not call the V2 implementation, or setPermissionsEnabled must be a no-op under V2.

Runtime client permission methods throw instead of deciding

Turning on ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 makes ClientPermissionsV2 the client evaluator for every realm, not only realms that opted into admin permissions. canExchangeTo, isPermissionsEnabled, and getPermissions unconditionally throw UnsupportedOperationException. canExchangeTo is the token-exchange authorization check (authorized client plus subject token) and used to return a boolean, including role-based allow or deny; a throw is a 500, not a deny. isPermissionsEnabled and getPermissions are still the client management-permissions API and are reachable from any parent method that was not overridden, so those calls 500 as well. Unimplemented V2 behavior needs to fail closed or keep the manage-clients role path, not throw. getEvaluationContext in this class is unused, so the exchange path was left unfinished.

Client resources are returned with a null display name

getResourceName only special-cases Users: the type resource becomes "All users" and other names are resolved to usernames, throwing ModelIllegalStateException if the user is gone. Client resources are stored under the internal client id (resolveClient returns client.getId()) and are created without a display name, so they hit return resource.getDisplayName() and come back null. The all-clients resource is named Clients and is not labeled "All clients". Permission listings for the new type show blank names, and a deleted client does not surface the missing-object error used for users.

testConfigureOnlyOneClient calls generateNewSecret and invalidateRotatedSecret on myclient and never puts the original secret back. realmAdminClient is injected for the class as client myclient; the sibling impersonation helper logs in with client secret mysecret. After rotation, refresh for that confidential client fails, so later methods in this class can 401 once the access token is no longer reused. testManageOnlyOneClient also renames myclient and removeDefaultClientScope without restoring either, and AfterEach only deletes scope permissions, so later methods share that leaked client state.

The new javadoc on requireView says it returns true if canView() returns true, but the method is void and throws ForbiddenException when the check fails, same as requireManage. requireViewClientScopes (line 102) has the same error: it says it returns true if canViewClientScopes() returns true. Implementors reading only the contract will treat these as predicates instead of enforcing checks.

This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() passes both VIEW and MANAGE to hasPermission and returns true if either scope is granted. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup authorizes only with requireManage(), so an admin who was granted view-only on groups can create top-level groups and can move an existing group to the top of the tree by posting its id. canManage(GroupModel) correctly requires MANAGE, and UserPermissions.canManage() does not treat view as manage. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

Member-view filter stores authorization resource ids, not group ids

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() is the set UsersResource.getUsersCount, UsersResource.searchForUser, and BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser apply as the groups whose members the caller may see. The findByType callback passes groupResource.getId() (the authorization resource primary key) both into hasPermission() and into the returned set. hasPermission() looks up resources by name, and per-group resources are named with the group id, so the lookup misses the group, falls back to the all-groups resource, and ignores the per-group view-members/manage-members grant. The ids placed in the session UserModel.GROUPS attribute are not group ids, and the schema resource named "Groups" is itself included by findByType. User search then matches nobody, so paginated results omit users the admin is allowed to see; when the set is empty, the query is not constrained and getUsersCount returns 0 while the list path only filters later in memory. Both connect this to missed per-group permissions, fallback to the all-groups resource, and incorrect user filtering or counts. The candidate's additional details do not change the core issue.

Per-group authz resources are created without a type

getOrCreateResource() creates the per-object resource and updates scopes, but never calls setType(resourceType). V1 GroupPermissions.initialize did set the type. GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() discovers groups with resourceStore.findByType(server, "Groups"), so individual group resources are invisible to that scan and view-members/manage-members grants never contribute real group ids to the user-search filter. Only the schema-level resource created in init(), which does set type, is found. Because the type is also unset, an evaluator that applies resource-type policies only to typed resources will not apply all-groups policies to these rows either.

AdminPermissions.registerListener still handles every GroupRemovedEvent by calling management().groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled. With ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 also enabled, groups() is now GroupPermissionsV2, and setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException. The listener is invoked from realm.removeGroup with no catch, so deleting any group (not only groups that have permissions) fails with a 500 and rolls back. V1 fine-grained admin authz is commonly enabled together with V2. If only V2 is enabled, the listener is not registered at all because it checks the V1 feature, so authorization resources created for a group by getOrCreateResource are never removed when the group is deleted. The same throw breaks the V1 management/permissions admin endpoint, which calls setPermissionsEnabled after requiring ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ.

All-groups policies are skipped once a per-group resource exists

hasPermission() evaluates only the per-group resource when findByName finds one, and loads the Groups type resource only when that lookup returns null. getOrCreateResource creates that row as soon as any permission references the group, including a different admin or a different scope such as view-members. After that, GroupPermissionsV2 never consults all-groups allow or deny policies for that group: an admin with all-groups MANAGE loses update, delete, and membership checks on it, and a negative all-groups policy does not deny a scope granted by the specific resource. Group listing no longer short-circuits on canView(), so those groups also disappear from an admin who only has all-groups view. testManageAllGroups only updates a group that has no specific resource, so only the fallback path is tested.

Existing admin-permissions clients never receive the Groups schema

init() returns immediately when the realm already has an admin-permissions client, so upgrade does not add the Groups resource type, the "Groups" all-resource, or the new scopes manage-membership, manage-members, and view-members. On those realms, creating a group permission fails: getScope throws ModelValidationException because the scope does not exist, and getOrCreateResource throws ModelException ("No scopes found") when attaching scopes. GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission then gets a null type resource from getResourceTypeResource and passes it to policyStore.findByResource and resource.getScopes(), which are not null-safe, so group list and permission checks for fine-grained admins throw NullPointerException instead of denying. This pull request contains no migration.

After evaluatePermission, GroupPermissionsV2 returns true for any permission whose scopes intersect the requested scopes. UserPermissionsV2, which this evaluator copies, ignores permissions whose resource id is not the resource just evaluated, because the result is not guaranteed to contain only that resource. Omitting the check here can apply a scope granted on another resource to the group being checked, widening view, manage, view-members, manage-members, or manage-membership beyond that group's policies.

V2 canView(GroupModel) does not reuse the no-arg canView() result, and GroupsResource.getGroups and GroupResource.getSubGroups dropped the previous canViewGlobal short-circuit. An admin whose access comes from an all-groups permission therefore runs a full authorization evaluation for every group on the page, even though each call falls back to the same Groups type resource. On realms with large group trees the groups admin API issues one policy evaluation, and several store queries, per group on every list request.

getResourceName() maps Users resources to the username, but a Groups resource falls through to resource.getDisplayName(). getOrCreateResource() stores the group id as the resource name and never sets a display name, so the authorization admin API shows a null name, or a raw id, for group permissions instead of the group name. After the group is deleted or renamed those resources stay unresolved, whereas a missing user at least throws ModelIllegalStateException.

The javadoc on requireManageMembers says it throws ForbiddenException if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false. The implementation throws when canManageMembers returns false. Those are different scopes (manage-membership versus manage-members), so the published contract on this permission interface is wrong.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)

CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider is specified to return the BouncyCastle or BCFIPS Provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is whichever JDK provider implements the default keystore type (typically SUN, or SunJSSE when the default type is PKCS12) and follows the keystore.type security property. Callers that pass this Provider into Signature.getInstance, Cipher.getInstance, or CertificateFactory.getInstance do not get BouncyCastle algorithms. PKCS7 padding, BCFKS, and other BC-only operations fail, or they silently run on a non-FIPS JDK provider. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null for this method and callers already null-check and fall back; a non-null SUN provider skips that fallback. This should return null or throw UnsupportedOperationException like the other unimplemented methods, not an unrelated JCA provider.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore's JDK provider instead of the expected BouncyCastle provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() is abstract, so existing CryptoProvider implementations crash

CryptoProvider is a public SPI implemented outside this interface (the default, Elytron, and FIPS artifacts, plus downstream crypto providers). order() was added as an abstract method with no default. An implementation compiled against the previous interface throws AbstractMethodError when ServiceLoader instantiates it and detectProvider sorts with CryptoProvider::order. That error aborts provider detection entirely, so Keycloak will not start even if a newer provider on the classpath would have been selected. A default method returning a low value (below AuthzClientCryptoProvider's 100 and the in-tree providers' 200) would keep existing implementations loadable and still prefer the updated providers.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding order() as an abstract method to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations that do not implement it. The candidate provides additional runtime consequences and a default-method remedy.

false_positives.candidate:
Tied crypto providers are chosen silently instead of failing startup

detectProvider used to throw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath, which stopped the server from running with an ambiguous crypto stack. It now sorts by CryptoProvider.order() descending and always returns the first entry, logging the rest only at debug. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so they tie. Stream.sorted is stable, so the winner is whichever jar ServiceLoader encounters first (classpath or module order), not an explicit preference. A deployment that accidentally contains both the default BouncyCastle provider and the FIPS provider — previously a startup error — will now boot and can run non-FIPS crypto, or drop Elytron in favor of BC, with no error and no info-level log. ServiceLoader also instantiates every provider before the sort, so the losing provider's constructor still registers JCA providers and mutates security properties, and the process continues in that mixed state. AuthzClientCryptoProvider at order 100 is correctly deprioritized, but that does not require ignoring a tie at the winning order. If several providers share the maximum order, startup should still fail and list them. Nothing in this change tests that selection.

AuthzClient.create permanently pins CryptoIntegration to its classloader

CryptoIntegration.init is process-global and returns immediately once a provider is set, so the first caller permanently chooses it. AuthzClient.create now calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) as a side effect of constructing a client. ServiceLoader therefore runs only against that classloader, not the thread context classloader and not the classloader a later server or application init would pass. If this runs first in a JVM where AuthzClient's classloader can see AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100) but not DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, or WildFlyElytronProvider — for example keycloak-common in a parent classloader and the real crypto module only in a child — the stub provider is installed and every later CryptoIntegration.init is a no-op. PEM, signature, certificate, AES, and truststore calls then throw UnsupportedOperationException, and the server no longer uses BouncyCastle or FIPS. Before this change, creating an AuthzClient did not initialize crypto, so the server's own init still selected the intended provider. A library constructor should not freeze detection, or a later init that finds a higher-order provider must be allowed to replace the stub.

ECDSA test never checks JCA DER or the real curve sizes

ECDSAAlgorithmTest builds one KeyPair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() and no ECGenParameterSpec, so the key is the JVM default curve (P-256 on SunEC). It then runs ES256, ES384, and ES512 against that same key and only asserts that asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(rs)) equals rs. It never checks that the DER matches the original Signature.sign() bytes, and it never calls Signature.verify on the converted DER. A codec that is self-inverse but not valid DER still passes, and integerToBytes silently pads or truncates to algorithm.getSignatureLength(), so a P-256 signature padded out to the ES512 length of 132 also round-trips. Because R and S stay about 32 bytes, sequence and integer lengths stay under 128, so the long-form length paths in ASN1Encoder.writeLength and ASN1Decoder.readLength — required for real P-521 signatures — are never executed. Provider ordering is also untested. The test should initialize secp256r1, secp384r1, and secp521r1 explicitly, assert the DER equals the JCA signature or verifies, and cover ServiceLoader selection.

When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Narrowed BuildIndex lock races same-key builds and clobbers the cache

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for the entire build, which serialized bleve.New and cache publication. The mutex is now taken only for b.cache[key] = idx. getOrCreateIndex in search.go is still check-then-build with no per-key lock (the TODO above it says so), so two searches, or a search and a watch event, for a namespace that was not prebuilt can both miss the cache and build at once. File-backed builds then call bleve.New on the same directory concurrently; that races inside bleve, and the loser fails with path-already-exists even though an index was created.
