false_positives.candidate:
Parallel index init shares err and can ignore build failures

searchSupport.init starts one errgroup goroutine per namespace, but every goroutine assigns the build result to the single outer err variable and returns that same variable. BuildIndex used to hold its cache mutex for the whole build, so those goroutines mostly ran one at a time; after the lock was narrowed they actually run in parallel and the unsynchronized err writes race. A goroutine whose build failed can observe nil after another goroutine's success overwrites err, return nil, and let errgroup.Wait succeed, so the server starts with that namespace missing from the index. The reverse also happens: a successful goroutine can return another goroutine's error and fail startup incorrectly. totalBatchesIndexed is incremented from the same goroutines without synchronization. Each goroutine needs its own error variable.

Index watch starts at the latest RV and drops writes made during the build

build returns the resource version observed while listing a namespace, and the comment on that return says watchers must apply every event since that version. init discards the returned version and then calls WatchWriteEvents, which samples the latest resource version at subscription time and only delivers newer rows. Creates, updates, and deletes that commit after a namespace was listed and before that subscription — expected when another HA replica writes during the long startup index build — are neither in the listed snapshot nor replayed. Updated documents stay stale in the search index, and deletes from that window remain searchable until a full rebuild. Namespaces are listed concurrently, so each list has its own version; the watch cursor has to be the earliest of those list versions, not the global maximum after every build finishes.

File indexes cannot be reopened, so eager init fails every restart

File-backed indexes are created with bleve.New on a stable path (Root/namespace/resource.group). bleve.New fails if that directory already exists, and this code never calls bleve.Open or deletes a leftover directory. If the builder fails, BuildIndex returns without closing the index or removing the partial directory. After the first successful file-backed build, or after a failed build that created the directory, the next process calls BuildIndex again, bleve.New fails, and NewResourceServer now aborts Init and refuses to construct the server. FileThreshold's zero value is 0, so any namespace with a positive count uses disk unless the caller sets a higher threshold. Startup must reopen or replace an existing directory, and error paths must delete partial indexes, or a normal restart cannot bring the storage server up.

Init failure returns nil without rolling back partial startup

NewResourceServer now calls Init and, on error, returns nil without calling the cancel func created above, lifecycle.Stop, or closing the blob bucket opened earlier in the constructor. If lifecycle.Init already opened the SQL database, those connections leak because the caller has no server value on which to call Stop. If search indexing succeeded and only the later watcher setup failed, search.init has already started a watch goroutine on context.Background that nothing will stop. Indexes already published into the caller-owned SearchBackend stay cached, so a retry that reuses that backend treats them as complete and skips rebuilding. Failure needs to stop lifecycle hooks, cancel background work, and drop partial indexes before returning the error.

Search watch loop ignores shutdown and panics when the event channel closes

After indexing, init starts a goroutine that reads WatchWriteEvents in a bare for loop and does not check the receive ok value. The watch context is context.Background, not the server context cancelled by Stop, so server shutdown does not stop the loop. The SQL poller closes that channel when the backend stops; the next receive yields a nil event, and handleEvent immediately dereferences evt.Type and panics, crashing the process during shutdown. If the backend is never stopped, the goroutine and poller leak for the rest of the process. Init now runs inside NewResourceServer, so this goroutine is created for every search-enabled server, including ones that are constructed and shut down without serving a request. The loop should use the server lifetime context and exit when the channel closes.

false_positives.candidate:
Rebalance kills the shared pool, then commits unprocessed messages

FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy, but close(), terminate(), and join() all call queue_pool.shutdown(). Arroyo handles revocation by close()+join() on the current strategy, then create_with_partitions() on the same factory. shutdown() sets each worker's shutdown flag and calls Queue.shutdown(), after which put() raises queue.ShutDown. The next strategy still uses that dead pool, so every submit fails to enqueue. submit()'s except block treats that failure as success: it add_offset/complete_offset and returns, and the new commit thread then commits those offsets (the factory wrapper adds 1, so the group offset moves past them). Results already sitting in the queue at revoke are abandoned and, on redelivery, dropped the same way. After the first rebalance, scale-in, or deploy, uptime results are never handled and will not be retried for the rest of the process. Give each assignment its own pool created in create_with_partitions, and only shut it down after that assignment has drained and committed; do not destroy a factory-owned pool from close(). Tests never close a strategy and call create_with_partitions again, so they miss this.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure

Each worker queue is created with queue.Queue() (maxsize 0, unbounded) and FixedQueuePool.submit() always put()s without blocking. poll() only records a gauge. The strategy docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever blocks the consumer thread. One slow subscription occupies its single worker while the consumer keeps reading that partition into memory; WorkItem also retains the full Kafka message, which the worker never reads. Commits stop at the oldest incomplete offset, so a stuck item also prevents committing every later message on the partition and those payloads cannot be released. Because poll() keeps returning, max.poll.interval is not exceeded and Kafka will not move the partition to a healthy consumer. The process can OOM and, on crash, must reprocess the entire uncommitted backlog. Bound the queues and block in submit() or poll() when a queue is full so the consumer actually applies backpressure.

Commit callback runs off the processing thread

_commit_loop is a daemon thread started from SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__ and calls the Arroyo commit callback every second while the processor thread is in consumer.poll() and strategy.submit(). librdkafka consumers are not thread-safe, and Arroyo expects commit to run on the processing thread; concurrent staging/commit and poll can drop offset updates or fault the consumer. close() also joins this thread before workers finish, so the last snapshot misses offsets that complete during shutdown and those messages are redelivered. Commit contiguous offsets from poll() on the processing thread, and do one final commit at the end of join() after queued work is idle, instead of using a side thread.

Shutdown does not drain queues and ignores join timeout

OrderedQueueWorker leaves its loop as soon as self.shutdown is true, and FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets that flag before Queue.shutdown(immediate=False). A worker blocked in get() processes at most one more item and then exits, so the rest of the queue is never handled. close() has already stopped the commit thread, so those offsets are not committed. join() ignores the timeout it is given, calls close(), and never raises TimeoutError, so Arroyo treats shutdown as complete and will not call terminate(). Workers are daemon threads and are joined one after another with a 5s timeout each, so 20 stuck workers block the consumer thread inside close/join for about 100 seconds (which can exceed max.poll.interval.ms) and can then be killed mid-handler when the process exits, after partial side effects and without running finally. A second close() or ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() calls Queue.shutdown() again, which raises queue.ShutDown and is logged as an error on every clean shutdown. join() should drain (or raise TimeoutError), commit, then stop workers, using one shared deadline.

Queue-pool tests race the already-running workers

test_stats_reporting asserts total_items > 0 immediately after submit, but the three workers are started in setUp and only append to a list, so they can drain all 10 items before get_stats() and fail the assertion on a fast run. test_offset_committing and test_offset_gaps_block_commits treat the first commit_event as proof that the final offset was committed. The commit loop fires about once a second and sets that event for whatever prefix is contiguous at that moment, so the assertion can observe a partial offset (for example 102, or 100 on the gap test) before the later commit updates it.

false_positives.candidate:
ZUNIONSTORE sums scores and breaks redelivery

The merge calls ZUNIONSTORE with no AGGREGATE, so Redis defaults to SUM. Members are the raw span payloads and scores are end_timestamp_precise. Kafka delivery is at-least-once: a retry ZADDs the same payload into the parent key and this script unions that key into the segment key that already holds the member. Each retry adds the timestamp again (T, 2T, 3T). The previous SUNIONSTORE path was idempotent. After the new 1000-span cap, ZPOPMIN keeps the inflated duplicates and drops spans that were ingested only once. Under the cap every member is still present, so the existing flush tests do not catch it. Pass AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN) so a retry keeps a real timestamp.

Segment keys changed from SET to ZSET with no migration

Span segment keys stay at span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id, but this write switched from SADD to ZADD, add-buffer.lua switched from SCARD/SUNIONSTORE to ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE, and _load_segment_data switched from SSCAN to ZSCAN. Redis raises WRONGTYPE when those commands hit the other type. TTL is 3600s and unflushed segments live at least until the 10s/60s flush. A rolling deploy runs both versions on the same keys, and after cutover leftover SET keys cannot be updated or scanned. process_spans then errors on every retry of that batch and can stall the partition until the key expires; flush_segments fails the same way, so those spans are never emitted. Version the key prefix or dual-handle existing sets before deploying.

Parent-redirect walk cap reduced from 10000 to 1000

The loop that follows span-buf:sr redirects used to run to 10000, with a comment that a deeper chain would not be joined onto the correct segment. It is now for i = 0, 1000 and the warning is gone. This limit is not the eviction cap: it is how many parent hops are resolved to compute set_span_id. A chain longer than 1000 spans, which the old code explicitly tolerated up to 10k and which large traces can produce when batches arrive one level at a time, stops at an intermediate parent. Those spans are merged into the wrong segment key and flushed apart from their root. Restore the previous bound unless there is a measured reason to lower it.

Over-cap eviction is silent, ignores config, and can drop the root

If the segment sorted set has more than 1000 members, ZPOPMIN deletes the lowest end_timestamp_precise scores and throws the members away. The limit is hardcoded and does not read SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (default 1001), which is now unused: the flush path that enforced it, logged the span count, and incremented spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded was removed. Dropped spans are not metered and not marked on the flushed payload, and the consumer still commits the Kafka offset, so the loss is permanent and invisible. There is also no exception for the segment span, so a root whose timestamp is among the lowest is deleted while the has-root-span flag can still be set and a partial segment is emitted as a normal one. Equal scores, which the tests all use, make ZPOPMIN break ties by raw payload bytes, so which spans survive is arbitrary. Pass max_segment_spans into the script, record a metric and a truncation marker, and do not evict the segment span.

No coverage for eviction, score order, or duplicate ingest

The insert-time cap is the point of this change, but every buffer test still inserts four spans that share end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0 and only checks flushed span ids. Those assertions still pass if ZPOPMIN never runs, if it drops the wrong members, if a second process_spans of the same payloads inflates ZUNIONSTORE scores, or if a segment larger than 1000 spans is returned in full. Add a case with more than 1000 distinctly scored spans (lowest scores removed, segment span kept) and a case that processes the same payloads twice.

Buffer glossary still calls segment keys complete sets

The glossary still says span-buf:s:* keys are Redis sets containing every span payload for a segment. They are now sorted sets written with ZADD and read with ZSCAN, and ZPOPMIN drops payloads once a segment exceeds 1000 spans, so the key is neither a set nor a complete segment. The algorithm notes above still describe merging sets and never mention eviction. Following the docstring leads operators to set commands (WRONGTYPE) and to treat a flushed segment as complete.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling uses the outer dataset and request query, not the query executed

`_get_event_stats` decides upsampling by calling `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` with the closed-over `dataset` and `request`, ignoring the `scoped_dataset` and `query` arguments it actually runs. Dashboard discover-split rewrites those arguments: error probes use discover and `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction`, transaction probes add `event.type:transaction`, and the outer dataset is often metrics-enhanced performance, which `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` always rejects. The helper only looks at `request.GET["query"]`, so every probe inherits the original request's decision. A transaction probe whose original query contains `event.type:error` is still rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)` and comes back empty or errors; `check_if_results_have_data` then reports no transactions and `save_split_decision` persists that on `DashboardWidget.discover_widget_split`. Later loads skip the check and keep the wrong split. Error-only split queries whose original request text did not contain `event.type:error` are never upsampled. Pass the executed dataset and query string into the check. The outer `except Exception` retry calls `_get_event_stats` again, so a Snuba failure from the rewrite is not avoided and surfaces as a 500 (the endpoint only catches `ValidationError`).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same core bug: the upsampling check uses the outer dataset rather than scoped_dataset, so dashboard discover-split queries can incorrectly skip upsampling when the original dataset is metrics. Its additional query-related claims do not negate this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Upsampled count drops events with no weight and truncates

`upsampled_count` is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`, and the helper comment says null checks are intentionally omitted. ClickHouse `sum` skips NULLs, so any error in an allowlisted project that has no `sample_weight` (historical events, events ingested before the column was filled, or unsampled events that should count as 1) contributes nothing. Enabling the allowlist can therefore make the series smaller than raw `count()`, including showing 0. `toInt64` truncates toward zero, so a fractional weight such as `1/0.3` is biased low on every bucket (one event at 3.333 becomes 3). If `sample_weight` is actually the rate 0.1 rather than the multiplier 10, `toInt64(sum(...))` is 0, not the 10 the new test expects. The aggregate needs a missing-weight default of 1 and rounding (for example `round(sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1)))`). With that default, mixed queries would not need the all-or-nothing allowlist gate, which today changes a project's displayed count depending on whether every other selected project is allowlisted.

Error-query check is a substring match and false-positives on negation

`_is_error_focused_query` lowercases `request.GET["query"]` and returns true when the substring `event.type:error` appears anywhere. That is true for `!event.type:error`, for `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, and for a quoted value such as `message:"event.type:error"`. On an allowlisted project set those queries rewrite `count()` to `sum(sample_weight)`. Non-error rows do not have a usable weight, so the stats request undercounts (NULLs add nothing) or fails in Snuba. The same check misses the usual discover error filter `!event.type:transaction` and list syntax such as `event.type:[error]`, so those error queries stay at the raw sampled count. The unit tests only cover the exact strings `event.type:error` and `event.type:transaction`, so the negation false positive is untested. Parse the search query and honor negation instead of substring matching.

Top-events ranking, equations, and count filters are not upsampled

Only the y-axis list is rewritten, and `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` replaces a column only when the entire string is `count()` after strip and lower. `top_events_timeseries` still gets `selected_columns` from `get_field_list`, `equations` from `get_equation_list`, and `orderby` from `get_orderby`, plus the raw `user_query`. Top-N is therefore ranked by sampled `count()` while the series uses `upsampled_count() as count`, so a heavily sampled group can be dropped from the top N, and an orderby that still names `count()` can fail the query because that aggregate was renamed. Aggregate conditions such as `count():>10` in the user query stay raw. Equation y-axes (`equation|count() / count_unique(user)`), `count() as <alias>`, `epm()`, and `eps()` are not rewritten either, so one response can mix upsampled and sampled series. Rewrite every count-based aggregate the query will run, or refuse those shapes while upsampling is on.

Allowlist cache is slower than options.get and cannot be invalidated

Every organization events-stats request now does a default-cache get (Redis in production) under `error_upsampling_eligible:{org}:{hash(sorted(project_ids))}`, and a set on miss, to avoid `options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist")`. That option read is already process-local memory, so this adds a network round trip and a high-cardinality key (one entry per distinct project-id set) on a hot endpoint. The cached boolean does not include the allowlist version. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called, and it can delete only one project-set key, so an allowlist edit cannot drop the other combinations. For up to 60 seconds after a project is removed, stats keep rewriting `count()` to `sum(sample_weight)` and can 500 or return weighted counts for projects that are no longer eligible; after a project is added, counts stay raw. The note on `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` says the allowlist is read fresh on every call so config changes apply immediately, which is false once this cache is in front. Read the option directly, or cache it in-process keyed by the allowlist contents and actually invalidate it.

upsampled_count is public, so the allowlist does not gate the feature

The new `SnQLFunction` is registered without `private=True`, unlike the internal aggregate immediately above it. The allowlist logic only rewrites a y-axis that is exactly `count()`; it does not block callers from requesting the function themselves. Any client can pass `yAxis=upsampled_count()` on discover and bypass the rollout. On datasets or projects where `sample_weight` is absent (transactions, spans, non-allowlisted projects) that same public function turns a user-controlled y-axis into a failed stats query. The aggregate should stay internal to the rewrite path so the allowlist is actually what enables it.

errors dataset always rewrites count() but the function is only added on discover

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns true for any `sentry.snuba.errors` query, and the endpoint then sends `upsampled_count()` to that dataset's query builder. The aggregate is only inserted into discover.py's `function_converter`. `sentry.search.events.builder.errors` is not changed, and `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest` never passes `dataset=errors` (it uses the default dataset plus `query=event.type:error`). If the errors dataset does not inherit Discover's function map, every allowlisted `dataset=errors` stats request fails with an unknown function as soon as the allowlist is non-empty. The string-level unit test does not run the query builder, so it would not catch that. Register the function on the errors dataset config and add a snuba test that uses `dataset=errors`.

Upsampling stats tests share one cache key and disagree on the allowlist

These tests patch `sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options` but not `sentry.utils.cache.cache`. Eligibility is cached for 60 seconds under a key built only from organization id and the project id set. All four tests use the same projects, so they share that key, while stubbing three different allowlists (both ids, one id, and empty) and expecting different counts (10 vs 1). This class's `setUp` never calls `cache.clear()` or deletes that key, and Django's `TestCase` does not clear the cache. If an earlier test cached true, `test_error_upsampling_with_partial_allowlist` and `test_error_upsampling_with_no_allowlisted_projects` still rewrite `count()` and their `count == 1` assertions fail; the reverse order makes the allowlisted test expect 10 and get 1. Mock or clear the cache in `setUp`.

Transaction upsampling test queries before the event is ingested

`test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events` calls `store_event` for a transaction and immediately GETs events-stats. `setUp` has to call `wait_for_event_count` before its queries, so ingestion is asynchronous here. The assertion that the first bucket `count` is 1 races the consumer and flakes at 0. Waiting for `wait_for_event_count(self.project.id, 1)` would also be wrong: `setUp` already stored an error in that project, so a count of 1 is satisfied before the transaction is written. Wait until that transaction is actually queryable (for example project event count 2, or a transaction-specific query) before asserting.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative checks reload full permissions from the DB per resource

Check only returns early when the cached permission set allows the request (line 131). Any cache hit that does not allow, and any cache miss, falls through to getIdentityPermissions, and the in-function cache read was removed from getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions, so that call always runs GetUserPermissions and reloads the user's full permission set. The new denial cache only suppresses a repeat of the exact same user, action, name, and parent. After that reload refreshes permCache, the next Check for a different resource this user cannot access still misses the denial cache, fails the scope check, and starts another full permission query. singleflight collapses only overlapping calls for the same user and action; once that call returns, the next distinct name queries again. Sequential authz of many dashboards or folders therefore becomes one DB permission load per denied resource per TTL instead of one load per user per action per 30s. In-proc clients now use NoopCache, so they no longer absorb repeats either. Random UIDs (including anonymous GETs) bypass the denial cache and can drive unbounded permission queries. Trust a negative result while the cached permission set is still fresh, and bypass it at most once per TTL rather than once per resource.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same asymmetric cache handling in Check: cached grants return immediately, while cached denials trigger a database permission lookup. The candidate emphasizes performance consequences rather than the golden comment's stale-grant security risk, but identifies the same underlying logic issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test still passes if the short-circuit is removed

TestService_CacheCheck subtest "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" claims the permission-cache fixture allows dash1 so that only the denial cache can explain the deny. The fixture is map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. checkPermission treats a false or missing scope as not allowed, and setupService's fake store returns no permissions, so Check still returns Allowed=false if the permDenialCache lookup is deleted. The comment says the entry allows access, but the value is false. Set that scope to true and assert the permission store is not called, otherwise a regression of the deny short-circuit is invisible.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same mismatch: the comment claims cached permissions allow dash1 access, but the scope is stored as false, so checkPermission treats it as denied. The additional explanation about masking a denial-cache regression is consistent with that issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key collides for UIDs that contain underscores

userPermDenialCacheKey joins name and parent with '_' (namespace.perm_<user>_<action>_<name>_<parent>). Dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, and those two fields sit next to each other, so different pairs encode to the same key. For example name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both end in _a_b_c for the same user and action. The cache only stores negatives, so a deny for one resource is returned for the other for 30s without checking permissions, and a user who can access one of them is incorrectly denied. Use an unambiguous encoding (length prefixes, a delimiter that cannot appear in UIDs, or a hash).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify ambiguous underscore-delimited concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey, allowing different component values to produce the same key and cause incorrect permission-denial cache hits. The candidate provides a concrete collision example matching the golden issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache pins non-authoritative denies for 30s and overrides later allows

Check returns Allowed=false immediately when permDenialCache contains the key, before consulting cached or current permissions. On any successful deny after the DB path, line 154 stores that denial for shortCacheTTL (30s) and nothing deletes it when a later permission reload would allow the same resource. The denial also wins over a positive permCache entry, so List (which uses the permission cache) can show a resource that Check still denies. This is not limited to authoritative DB denies: checkPermission returns false when the cached folder tree does not yet contain a newly created parent, so an ancestor folder grant is recorded as a denial and keeps failing after the folder cache would have allowed it. getUserPermissions is singleflighted and does not re-read after the in-flight query, so a Check that joins a permission load started before a create/grant can observe the pre-grant snapshot and then pin that stale deny for 30s. That recreates the creator-cannot-open-the-new-dashboard failure, and it extends false denies past permission-cache expiry when a grant follows an earlier deny. Do not write a denial when the result depends on a stale folder tree or a shared in-flight snapshot, and invalidate denial entries whenever permissions are reloaded.

List still serves stale permissions for newly created dashboards and folders

List now returns getCachedIdentityPermissions on a hit and only calls getIdentityPermissions on a miss. Check was changed so a cached set that does not include the requested resource is reloaded from the DB, but List still treats the cached set as complete for the whole shortCacheTTL (30s). A creator whose permission cache was filled before the create will not see the new dashboard or folder in list results until that entry expires, which is the failure this PR describes for any caller that fetches via List rather than Check. Use the same freshness rule as Check, or invalidate the permission cache when a dashboard or folder permission is created.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Re-link crashes when metadata has no sender

On the re-link path the code indexes integration.metadata['sender']['login'] with no guard. build_integration only stores sender when pipeline state already has it, and this flow never writes github_authenticated_user into metadata. An ACTIVE Integration without a sender dict — older rows, rows created only by build_integration, or a webhook that stored sender under a different shape — raises KeyError or TypeError instead of the installation error page. The setup popup 500s and the re-link cannot finish.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify unguarded access to integration.metadata['sender']['login'], which raises a KeyError when sender metadata was not set during integration creation. The candidate adds context but describes the same underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
installation_id is persisted before the OAuth state check

OAuthLoginView copies installation_id from the query string into pipeline state before it verifies that state equals pipeline.signature. bind_state writes the session immediately (the happy path depends on that, because installation_id must survive the redirect to GitHub). A request that then fails the state check still returns the error page, but the overwritten installation_id remains. PipelineAdvancerView is CSRF-exempt and this endpoint is a top-level GET, so a cross-site navigation to /extensions/github/setup/?installation_id=<attacker>&state=invalid is enough to poison an in-progress install. The victim's later successful OAuth callback does not carry installation_id, and GitHubInstallation prefers the stored value. The victim's organization is then linked using the attacker's installation id.

Installer identity is not checked on first install

The new check that the OAuth login matches metadata['sender']['login'] runs only when an Integration row already exists and has no OrganizationIntegration. If Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist, dispatch returns pipeline.next_step() and never reads github_authenticated_user. That is the normal first-install path: the installation webhook that records sender is asynchronous and often loses the race with the browser redirect, and build_integration only copies state['sender'] — it never receives or compares github_authenticated_user. Supplying an attacker installation_id (setup URL or the poisoned pipeline state) before that row exists links it to the victim's Sentry organization with no user check. The guarantee in the PR — fail on a mismatch between the OAuth user and the user who installed the GitHub App — is not enforced for new installations. The new test posts the webhook first, so it never covers this path.

Non-active Integration rows can no longer be reinstalled

Previously, an Integration that existed but had no OrganizationIntegration always continued to pipeline.next_step(), which re-fetches the GitHub installation and reactivates the record. The new lookup requires status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE and turns DoesNotExist into the generic authenticity error. ObjectStatus includes DISABLED, PENDING_DELETION, and HIDDEN, so a leftover non-active row with no org link — a normal uninstall leftover — now blocks reinstall. The message tells the user the request could not be verified and to restart, which cannot succeed until the row is deleted out of band.

Token exchange omits redirect_uri sent on authorize

The authorize redirect includes redirect_uri, but the code exchange posts only code, client_id, and client_secret. RFC 6749 section 4.1.3 requires the token request to repeat redirect_uri when it was included in the authorization request, and the values must be identical. GitHub's POST /login/oauth/access_token documents the same parameter and rejects mismatches (redirect_uri_mismatch or an invalid/expired code). The new tests stub that URL and return a token no matter the body, so they stay green if GitHub rejects the exchange and every real install stops on the generic error page. The authorize URL is also built by string interpolation rather than urlencode, so the redirect_uri GitHub records may not byte-match a later form-encoded value.

OAuth network failures skip the installation error page

safe_urlopen of the token endpoint and the following get_user_info call sit outside the try/except that maps a bad token body to the installation error page. A timeout, connection error, or ApiError from either call propagates as an unhandled 500 in the setup popup. This change is supposed to render github-integration-failed.html when GitHub cannot mint a token or the user cannot be identified; that page is only reached when body parsing fails or access_token/login is missing.

installation-not-found test no longer hits the GitHub 404 path

test_installation_not_found used to request setup_path with an installation_id and assert build_integration's 404 text "The GitHub installation could not be found." It now overwrites that response with a second request whose state is ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, not the pipeline signature the other tests lock in (9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3), and asserts the generic "Invalid installation request." string. Unlike the updated happy-path tests it never calls init_path, so there is no session pipeline; PipelineAdvancerView redirects to / with "Invalid request.", which does not contain the new expected bytes. If a pipeline did exist, the wrong state is rejected in OAuthLoginView and the installations API is never called, so a regression in the 404 handling would not be caught.

User-mismatch test posts a webhook with a stale signature

test_github_user_mismatch changes INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE (installation id and sender.login) but sends a static X-Hub-Signature of sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486, the digest of the unmodified fixture. The webhook view HMACs the raw body, so this delivery is rejected and never creates an Integration whose sender is attacker; the assert resp.status_code == 204 fails when verification is enabled. The test then reuses state 9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3, captured for the default org, after login_as(user_2) and a new organization, and asserts the same "Invalid installation request." string that OAuthLoginView returns for a state mismatch. Neither a pass nor a fail shows that the sender comparison ran.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation treats wrapped isEnabled() as the DB flag

update() loads the previous identity provider with getById() and passes that instance to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(). With the organization feature on, getById() does not return the persisted row; it returns the wrapper from createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(), whose isEnabled() is false whenever the IdP has an organization id and the organization is missing, the organization is disabled, or OrganizationProvider.isEnabled() is false, even if the IdP's own enabled flag is still true. true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:

The flag has no effect, yet IsEnabledGlobally is still called before either return. false_positives.candidate:
Live SQL path still builds DuckDB statements and fails as a parse error

UnmarshalSQLCommand, the existing server-side expression entry point, never applies the new disable. NewSQLCommand always calls sql.TablesList (pkg/expr/sql_command.go:30). TablesList interpolates the user expression into a DuckDB statement, SELECT json_serialize_sql('...'), after only doubling single quotes (pkg/expr/sql/parser.go:24-26) and passes that string to RunCommands. The replacement DB always returns an error (pkg/expr/sql/db.go:16), so DuckDB is not executed and CVE-2024-9264 is not currently reachable here, but that stub error is the only control on this path. This change is the in-repo fix for critical CVE-2024-9264, but no test was added or updated. Restoring a DuckDB-backed RunCommands, or changing the inverted enableSqlExpressions helper so the flag turns the ReadQuery path back on, would not be caught. Manual checks mentioned in the PR description are not a substitute for a regression test on a patch intended to be cherry-picked across release branches.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write path never rechecks cache and can clear a good entry

In pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go, GetWebAssets drops its read lock and at line 48 takes entryPointAssetsCacheMu for the entire load (the assets-manifest file read, and readWebAssetsFromCDN if that branch runs) without reading entryPointAssetsCache again. Every caller that saw a nil cache therefore repeats that I/O while holding the write lock, so concurrent startup or dev calls serialize and the read-fast path blocks behind them. Line 69 then always stores the result, including when the load failed and result is nil. A caller that loses the race to a successful load can overwrite the published cache with nil and return an error even though assets were already loaded. After the write lock is acquired, return the existing pointer when Env is not Dev and the cache is non-nil, and only assign entryPointAssetsCache when the load succeeds.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same incomplete double-checked locking bug: GetWebAssets does not re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock, even though another goroutine may have populated it. The additional consequences and suggested fix do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

Successful cleanup batches are logged at Error with every ID

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log every batch with r.log.Error (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including the full ID slice, the SQL condition, and an err value that is already known to be nil. These fire even when the batch is empty, so an idle instance emits error-level lines on every cleanup cycle for age, count, and orphan-tag passes. Error is always emitted at production log levels, so this will flood logs, trip error-rate alerts, and serialize up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs (the new test uses 32767) on the hot path between the SELECT and the DELETE. That I/O also widens the race window of the split statements. These are leftover debug traces and should be removed; do not keep them at Error, and do not log the ID list.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify debug-style cleanup logging at Error level as inappropriate because it pollutes production error logs. The candidate adds details and consequences but addresses the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

CleanUpService.Run now uses time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1) instead of 10 minutes. The PR is about splitting annotation cleanup statements to avoid MySQL deadlocks; this schedule change is unrelated and undocumented. clean() still applies a 9-minute timeout, which only makes sense with the old 10-minute period so a run finishes before the next tick. At 1 minute, every cleanup job (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, and query history) runs up to 10x more often. If a run lasts longer than a minute, time.Ticker drops ticks and the next clean() starts immediately, so a slow annotation cleanup can run back-to-back with no gap and continuously load the database. Revert this to 10 minutes unless the frequency change is an intentional, documented product decision.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the cleanup ticker change from 10 minutes to 1 minute and warn that more frequent cleanup execution can increase database load and contention. The candidate adds details but addresses the same underlying performance concern.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite IN-list is built with quadratic string concatenation

When the database is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is above 999, deleteByIDs interpolates IDs into DELETE ... WHERE id IN (...). The list is built with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside the loop, which copies the entire growing string on every iteration. That is O(n^2) allocations on the path added specifically for large batches (the new test sets the batch size to 32767, and the setting is user-configurable with no upper bound here). Tens of thousands of IDs produce gigabytes of intermediate strings, GC pauses, and a cleanup stall or OOM, which defeats a larger batch size. Build the clause with strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt into a buffer.

Max-count cleanup can delete annotations that should be kept

Count-based retention selects IDs with ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT batch OFFSET maxCount, then deleteByIDs removes those IDs in a later autocommit statement with no re-check that they are still outside the cap. The previous single-statement DELETE evaluated the OFFSET atomically with the delete, so a row that no longer fell past MaxCount could not be removed. If newer annotations (the ones the OFFSET skipped) are deleted between the SELECT and the DELETE — by a user, the API, or another instance — the already-selected IDs can now sit inside the retention window and are still deleted. Those annotations are permanently lost and the configured max count is not honored. Concurrent inserts only under-delete, which the next cycle can fix; this race over-deletes, which the next cycle cannot undo. The comment on the age path only mentions under-deletion from inserts. The Error log of the full ID list between the two statements makes the window larger. The DELETE needs to be conditional on the row still being past the cap, or the data-loss window has to be an explicit accepted risk.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful deletes record the object name as the metric kind

On the delete success path, recordStorageDuration is called with the object name as its third argument (line 106). Every other call in this file, including the delete error path on line 103, passes options.Kind there, and these duration helpers are Prometheus metrics registered from the registry passed into NewDualWriter, with that argument as the kind label alongside mode and method. A distinct series per deleted object is unbounded cardinality and can exhaust Prometheus memory once mode 3 is enabled. Success and error delete series also cannot be joined. Pass options.Kind, as the error path does.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same inconsistency: the delete success path passes the object name to metrics recording instead of options.Kind, unlike the other methods and the delete error path.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes are canceled when the request ends

Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection perform the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is derived with context.WithTimeoutCause from the incoming request context (Create line 51, Update line 135, Delete line 110, DeleteCollection line 163). A child context is canceled as soon as its parent is. net/http cancels the request context when ServeHTTP returns, which is immediately after these methods return the unified-storage result, so the 10s timeout never applies and Legacy.Create/Update/Delete typically fail with context.Canceled before the DB write finishes. Mode 3 exists so legacy storage stays current enough to roll back; those safety writes will systematically fail in production, and nothing retries them. The goroutines also discard the legacy error without logging, unlike the previous synchronous implementation, so the divergence is invisible aside from a metric. Detach with context.WithoutCancel (not context.Background(), which would drop user/org/trace values) before applying a timeout, and log the legacy error.

Unordered goroutines can resurrect or revert legacy objects

Every successful Create (line 50), Update (line 134), Delete (line 108), and DeleteCollection (line 161) starts an independent goroutine with no per-resource queue, generation check, or in-flight tracking. Goroutines for the same object run in parallel and can finish out of order. A create followed quickly by a delete can delete on legacy first (NotFound) and then create, resurrecting an object that unified storage has already removed. Two updates can commit the newer spec and then the older one, rolling the safety copy backward. On rollback to legacy reads, users would see deleted or stale objects. Serialize legacy writes per resource and reject a write whose unified-storage resourceVersion/generation is older than what legacy already applied.

Legacy update no longer stores the object written to unified storage

Update passes the caller's original objInfo into Legacy.Update (line 139) after Storage.Update has already applied it. The code this PR replaces loaded the unified object, computed UpdatedObject once, and passed that exact result to both stores via updateWrapper. That snapshot is required because mode 3 reads come from unified storage, so the client's resourceVersion and any patch base belong to the unified copy, not the legacy copy. Legacy.Update will call UpdatedObject again against the legacy object and enforce the unified resourceVersion, which conflicts or yields a different spec whenever the stores differ. Most updates will fail to land in legacy, so the rollback copy stops tracking writes. Write the object returned by Storage.Update into legacy instead of replaying objInfo. Create has the same shape at line 55: it forwards the pre-write input obj rather than the created object, so server-side defaults present only on the returned object are not what legacy stores.

Storage failures and legacy delete-collection hit the wrong metric

When Storage.Create fails, line 45 calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration, and the observed interval is the failed storage call. Storage.Update's error path does the same at line 129. The async legacy DeleteCollection path at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration for a legacy operation. Unified-storage create/update failures are counted as legacy failures and omitted from storage error latency, while legacy delete-collection outcomes are attributed to unified storage. During a mode 3 migration, alerts will point at the wrong store. Use recordStorageDuration on the storage error paths and recordLegacyDuration for the legacy delete-collection goroutine.

NotFound from unified storage skips the legacy delete

Delete returns immediately on any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound (lines 101-104), and never starts the legacy delete. The previous implementation treated unified NotFound as non-fatal and still deleted from legacy. If an earlier legacy delete failed or lost the race with a later create, a client retry gets NotFound from unified storage (the source of truth) and the legacy object is left in place. After a rollback to legacy reads, that object reappears. A NotFound from unified storage should still attempt the legacy delete and ignore a legacy NotFound, since the client-facing error remains the unified result.

Destroy closes stores while legacy goroutines may still be writing

Destroy calls Storage.Destroy and Legacy.Destroy immediately and does not track the goroutines started by Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Apiserver shutdown can destroy legacy storage while those goroutines are still inside Legacy.Create/Update/Delete, which can panic on a closed backend or leave a half-applied safety write. Track in-flight legacy writes with a WaitGroup and wait for them in Destroy before tearing the stores down.

Unit tests never observe the async legacy write

TestMode3_Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection set legacy mock expectations but return as soon as the unified-storage call returns (Create at line 65). They never wait for the goroutine, never call AssertExpectations, and never check that legacy was invoked with the persisted object. Both mocks share one testify Mock, so the two Create expectations are interchangeable and a test passes even if the legacy call is skipped. They also use context.Background(), which is never canceled, so they cannot catch request-context cancellation. Inject a synchronous executor or wait for the goroutine, assert the legacy call and its arguments, and add a case whose parent context is already canceled.

Mode 3 playlist tests assume legacy is updated before the handler returns

The new mode 3 cases (file storage at line 133 and unified storage at line 192) call doPlaylistTests, which immediately lists and gets via the legacy /api/playlists endpoint after k8s create, update, and delete. Modes 0-2 mirror those writes synchronously, which is why that comparison works; mode 3 mirrors them only after the handler returns. The legacy read can therefore observe a missing or stale playlist and fail or flake, especially once the request context cancels the legacy write. If that endpoint no longer reads legacy storage, the new cases never check that the safety write landed at all. Wait until the legacy write is visible, or assert it through a hook, before comparing the two APIs.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Filtered Grafana rows are rendered without a key

FilterViewResults maps each result to a list child and previously set key={key} on GrafanaRuleLoader. The replacement GrafanaRuleListItem omits key, while the datasource and unknown branches still set it. React reconciles Grafana rows by index. RuleActionsButtons holds silence-drawer and clone redirect state on the row, so loading more results or refreshing the filtered list can attach that state to the wrong rule.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing React key prop on GrafanaRuleListItem rendered in a list and the resulting reconciliation issues when list contents or order change.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item is a no-op in the list view

AlertRuleMenu shows "Silence notifications" from prom-rule abilities and does not require a ruler rule. handleSilence only sets showSilenceDrawer. The drawer is mounted only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true, and the list calls RuleActionsButtons with promRule and no ruler rule, so the click never opens SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer. Users get an enabled Silence action that does nothing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: list views pass only promRule to RuleActionsButtons, allowing the Silence menu action via Prom abilities, but the drawer requires a Grafana Ruler rule and therefore never renders when clicked.

false_positives.candidate:
Duplicate is authorized by the ability source that has no rule

canDuplicate is the OR of the ruler ability and the Grafana prom ability, and a missing rule is not treated as "no opinion". useRulerRuleAbilities(undefined) still marks Duplicate supported whenever the ruler is available, because isPluginProvidedRule(undefined) is false and allowance is only the global Grafana create permission. useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(skipToken) does the same: skipToken is turned into undefined, useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities then sets MaybeSupported to AlwaysSupported, and Duplicate is allowed for anyone with Grafana AlertingRuleCreate. The permissive side wins. In the new list, plugin-provided rules therefore show Duplicate even though the prom path correctly denies it. In any AlertRuleMenu caller that has a cloud or other non-Grafana prom rule (or no prom rule), skipToken still grants Duplicate from the Grafana create permission, including when the ruler path says duplication is unsupported or the user lacks external-rule write. The menu item does not need a ruler rule, so the click starts the clone flow for a rule that should not be offered.

Federated rule groups are no longer immutable

useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false. The previous isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) check was removed, and RuleGroupIdentifierV2 does not carry source_tenants, so the TODO cannot be evaluated with the data this hook receives. immutableRule is therefore never set for Mimir/GEM federated groups. Edit, delete, pause, and restore stay enabled for those rules in every consumer of these hooks, not only the new list. Users can change or delete cross-tenant federated rules that the UI previously blocked, which can break multi-tenant evaluation or drop rules the normal editor cannot represent.

Delete never appears in the ruler-less list view

The Delete item is rendered only when canDelete && rulerRule. GrafanaRuleListItem passes only promRule into RuleActionsButtons, so rulerRule is undefined and Delete is omitted even when useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities allows it. The list handler already deletes via the prom-derived identifier and ignores the ruler-rule argument, so the guard drops a working action. Users with delete permission cannot delete Grafana-managed rules from the list.

Pause is unreachable without a ruler rule

The pause item is still rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) is true, and MenuItemPauseRule requires that ruler payload. The list view no longer fetches or passes a ruler rule, so Pause/Resume never appears even when the new prom ability says pause is supported and allowed. Removing the guard alone would pass undefined into MenuItemPauseRule. After this change, pausing or resuming an alert from the list is impossible.

Recording rules lose export, pause, and restore

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities gates ModifyExport, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently on prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule. The ruler hook it replaces uses rulerRuleType.grafana.rule, which is true for Grafana recording rules as well. Recording rules are Grafana-managed, share isPaused / is_paused with alerting rules, and previously could be exported. In the list view Export is hidden for every recording rule, and pause/restore stay unsupported even for users who can edit them.

View links drop returnTo

The deleted list item built the view href with createReturnTo() so the rule detail page could link back to the current list URL, including filters and search. The new href is /alerting/grafana/${uid}/view with no returnTo query param. Opening a rule from the filtered or grouped list and using the in-app back link lands on the default list instead of restoring the user's place.

Menu test locks in the incomplete action set

The More-menu test grants AlertingRuleDelete and folder update/delete, defines a delete selector, and then expects exactly four items: silence, copy link, duplicate, and export. It never clicks Silence and never asserts Delete or Pause. That count matches the current bugs (Delete and Pause omitted, Silence not required to open a drawer) and will fail a fix that shows the missing actions, so CI freezes the incomplete menu. Nothing covers plugin-provided or cloud rules, which is what would catch Duplicate being granted by an empty ability source.

Shard splitting interpolates every query twice

runSplitQuery now always maps targets through datasource.applyTemplateVariables before grouping and execution. runShardSplitQuery does the same (shardQuerySplitting.ts:52) and then, for every shard group, calls runSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163) with targets that are already interpolated and rewritten by interpolateShardingSelector. Substitution therefore runs twice on every shard-split query. The updated shard test locks this in by expecting applyTemplateVariables 5 times for one target (once up front, once per group) and stubs an idempotent string replace, so it never fails.

applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent: it both expands variables and injects request.filters into the LogQL. The second call sees the already substituted text plus the __stream_shard__ selector. Ad hoc filters are applied again onto a selector that was not the input the injector first rewrote, so matchers are duplicated and can be attached in the wrong place, producing invalid LogQL or a selector that no longer matches the shard values fetched on the first pass. Template replacement also does not rescan substituted values within one pass, so a label or line-filter value such as team-$env is left intact the first time and then expanded on the second pass if env is a dashboard variable. The same query with shard splitting off is interpolated only once, so shard splitting silently returns different streams. Interpolate once: keep a single applyTemplateVariables step for shard grouping, and skip it inside runSplitQuery when the caller has already prepared the targets.

Shard path no longer pre-expands $__range, so those queries are not time-split

runShardSplitQuery used to call interpolateVariablesInQueries(request.targets, request.scopedVars), which substitutes every scoped variable, including $__range, $__range_s, and $__range_ms, against the original request range. It now calls applyTemplateVariables, which deliberately strips __range, __range_s, __range_ms, __interval, and __interval_ms out of scoped vars so those macros stay in the expression for the backend.

The still-macro expressions are passed into runSplitQuery. querySupportsSplitting (querySplitting.ts:282-288) refuses to time-split any expression that still contains $__range, because the backend would otherwise interpolate it with the chunk time range. Previously the macro was already a constant full-range duration, the guard did not match, and the query was still chunked with a correct lookback. After this change, a shard-split metric query such as count_over_time({job="x"}[$__range]) over a multi-day dashboard range is sent as one unsplit request. The range value stays correct, but queries that previously completed via chunking can now hit Loki's max query duration or time out. $__interval / $__interval_ms are also no longer baked in from the original scoped vars, so the backend expands them per sub-request instead of using the dashboard interval. The new tests stub templateSrv.replace with a blind replace of $__auto and $step, so they never observe this. Expand range macros against the original scoped vars before the splitting decision (while still using applyTemplateVariables for step, legend, and ad hoc filters), or explicitly accept the no-split behavior and test it.

Expressions that interpolate to empty are no longer dropped before sharding

The previous shard entry point interpolated first and then dropped targets with a falsy expr. The new code filters on query.expr and !query.hide and only then calls applyTemplateVariables, with no second filter. A target whose expression is only a template variable that resolves to an empty string (a common optional dashboard variable) used to be removed and not executed. It is now passed into splitQueriesByStreamShard and groupTargetsByQueryType, which calls getSelectorForShardValues on that empty expression and languageProvider.fetchLabelValues for __stream_shard__. runSplitQuery later drops empty expressions, so the target is not queried, but the label lookup still runs and failures are only logged. If selector extraction throws, groupTargetsByQueryType rejects and the .then at shardQuerySplitting.ts:213 has no .catch, so the query observable never emits or completes and the panel hangs. Filter again after applyTemplateVariables, as the old interpolate-then-filter order did.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check races with the insert

When deviceLimit > 0, CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active rows for the last 30 days in one session and, if count < deviceLimit, performs INSERT ... ON CONFLICT in a second WithDbSession. There is no shared transaction, row lock, or conditional insert, so the cap is not atomic. Concurrent new devices — many browsers opening a shared anonymous dashboard, or every instance's cold cache after a restart — can all observe a count under the limit and all insert. The extra rows stay inside the 30-day window and can keep refreshing through updateDevice, so the overshoot persists until those devices age out or are deleted on login. Nothing later reconciles the table back down to the configured limit. The count and the write need to be one atomic operation that inserts only when this device_id already exists or the active count is still below the limit.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass a non-atomic device count check and insert devices beyond the configured limit. The candidate also recommends making the check and insert atomic, consistent with the golden comment's transaction or lock suggestion.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit denials are cached as successful tags

tagDeviceUI stores the device key (anon-device:<deviceID>) with SetDefault before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns, and a cache hit returns nil without touching the database. The default TTL is 29 minutes and the cache is process-local. This PR only rejects anonymous access when TagDevice returns anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached, so the first over-limit request for a new device is denied and leaves that key cached; every later request within the TTL skips the limit check, is not inserted or counted, and still receives an anonymous identity. Any other tagging error (count/insert failure, context cancel) is treated as non-fatal by Authenticate, but the poisoned key turns the following attempts into successes, so one transient database error also disables enforcement for 29 minutes. After expiry a single request fails and access is allowed again. The configured cap therefore does not limit anonymous sessions. Cache only after a successful write, and a cached denial must keep returning ErrDeviceLimitReached rather than nil.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same premature cache insertion in tagDeviceUI: an ErrDeviceLimitReached denial leaves the device cached, causing subsequent requests to bypass enforcement until the 29-minute TTL expires.

false_positives.candidate:
Device limit is skipped when the client omits the device header

Anonymous.Authenticate denies access only when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. TagDevice returns nil without consulting deviceLimit when X-Grafana-Device-Id is missing, and again when network.GetIPFromAddress fails (invalid RemoteAddr or forwarded address). Those requests are not counted and still get a full anonymous identity with the configured anonymous org role. The header is optional and client-supplied; nothing in this path mints a server-side device id, and Anonymous.Test always returns true, so any unauthenticated request can use this client. A script, API client, or browser that omits the header — including one that was just denied and retries without it — bypasses the cap entirely, while UI clients that send the header are restricted. If device_limit is meant to restrict anonymous access, it has to run on every anonymous authentication, not only on requests that opt into device tagging.

Wire provider signatures changed without updating generated injectors

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService no longer takes anonstore.AnonStore; it now takes db.DB and builds the store internally with cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit. ProvideAnonDBStore gained a bare int64 device-limit argument. Both are Google Wire providers. The previous signature required Wire to supply an AnonStore and pass it into ProvideAnonymousDeviceService, which is what pkg/server/wire_gen.go still does — that file is not in this diff. Those generated calls will not compile. Regenerating Wire is not enough while ProvideAnonDBStore remains in the provider set, because Wire cannot inject an unnamed int64. Remove ProvideAnonDBStore from the set (the store is already constructed inside ProvideAnonymousDeviceService) and regenerate wire_gen.go before merge.

Anonymous sign-in now blocks on device tagging

TagDevice previously ran in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout, so a slow anon_device write could not delay authentication. Authenticate now calls it synchronously on the request context before returning an identity, including when AnonymousDeviceLimit is 0 (the default), where the new limit branch is skipped and the call is only an upsert. The 29-minute per-process cache hides this in steady state, but a restart or deploy clears the cache and every anonymous request then waits on the database during sign-in. With a limit configured, each of those requests also runs COUNT(*) over the 30-day window before the user is admitted. A slow anon_device table, or row locks from DeleteDevicesOlderThan, now stalls anonymous page loads and API calls instead of a background goroutine. Do the synchronous round-trip only when a configured limit must allow or deny the request.

Device-limit test never checks existing devices or auth enforcement

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit inserts one row under the limit and asserts that a second new device id is rejected by the store. It never checks that a device already inside the 30-day window can still be updated once count >= deviceLimit, which is the updateDevice path existing anonymous users depend on. A bad WHERE clause or a RowsAffected == 0 false negative would lock out every anonymous user at the cap and this test would still pass. It also never calls TagDevice or Anonymous.Authenticate, so the local-cache short-circuit, a missing X-Grafana-Device-Id, and the new auth denial are all untested. The test stays green even if every retry is granted anonymous access. Cover existing-device refresh at the cap, repeated denial for a new device through TagDevice, and Authenticate both with and without the device header.

device_limit is undocumented and 0 silently disables it

auth.anonymous device_limit is parsed in readAuthSettings but not added to conf/defaults.ini or the configure-grafana docs. MustInt64(0) means enforcement is off, because the store only checks the cap when deviceLimit > 0; a negative or unparseable value also becomes unlimited, with no startup error. The cap counts devices whose updated_at is inside a hardcoded 30-day window, not the 61-day cleanup retention. Operators cannot discover the key, can set 0 expecting to allow no devices and instead disable the control, and cannot tell which devices consume a slot. Add the key to conf/defaults.ini with that default and document the 30-day active-device window and the 0/negative = disabled behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback bundles are not loaded on the translation path

I18n::Backend::Fallbacks resolves SiteSetting.default_locale and :en inside the backend, but the on-demand loader only runs for the active locale. I18n.translate (line 68) calls load_locale(config.locale) and never consults I18n.fallbacks, and backend fallback lookups do not go back through I18n.translate, so those YAML files stay unloaded. The new ensure_loaded! helper is only called from ApplicationController#set_locale. Mailers, jobs, rake tasks, console use, and I18n.with_locale / I18n.t(locale:) that never hit that filter therefore miss fallback strings and return a missing-translation result even when the site locale or English has the key. Argument-less lookups then store that failure in the process-wide LRU (line 74). Hot keys are not evicted, so one early lookup permanently poisons later requests in the same process even after ensure_loaded! has loaded the files.

Translation cache key ignores dynamic fallback locale

FallbackLocaleList#[] re-reads SiteSetting.default_locale on every lookup so the fallback language can change without a restart, but the accelerator cache key is only "#{key}#{config.locale}#{backend.object_id}". Nothing clears @cache when the site locale changes. Argument-less I18n.t results — including strings taken from the previous default locale and cached missing-translation placeholders — remain in the 300-entry LRU, and frequently used keys are never evicted. After an admin changes default_locale, users whose own locale lacks those keys keep seeing the old fallback language until the process is restarted. Interpolated calls skip the cache, so the same copy can also disagree with itself depending on whether it has interpolations.

No tests for fallback order, loading, or cache interaction

The new user-locale → SiteSetting.default_locale → :en chain, ensure_loaded!, and the accelerator cache have no coverage. Fallbacks are now installed in every environment (previously only production/profile), so tests that expected a missing non-English key to raise or return a missing-translation string will silently get English instead, and the job/mailer load gap and stale-cache-after-default-locale-change bugs above would not be caught. A controller example and a non-request I18n.t (after setting a non-English locale whose fallback files are not yet loaded) need to assert both the fallback order and that a miss is not cached before the fallback bundles are loaded.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plugin request logs drop traceID

LoggerMiddleware used to append traceID to every "Plugin Request Completed" line (eventName=grafana-data-egress) via tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false), which includes the ID even when the span is not sampled. That call was removed with the tracing import. The attributes now stored by ContextualLoggerMiddleware are only endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname, and the new plugins/log FromContext wrapper does not add a trace ID either. The UI sits on a blank page (and, with the off-by-one page count, may show 2/2 for a list that now fits on one page) until the admin clicks Previous.
