true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grant shortcuts are not validated as 2-character unique codes

Access-token ids are a fixed 6-character prefix (session type, token type, grant shortcut, 2 characters each) plus ':' plus the raw id. The decoder rejects any other prefix length. postInit stores each grant shortcut with no check that it is non-null, exactly 2 characters, free of ':', or unique beyond a map-size comparison. OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut's javadoc says shortcuts are 'usually like 3-letters', which cannot be represented in this format. A custom grant that follows that javadoc still passes the size check, and encodeTokenId will issue ids such as onrtabc:<uuid>. Decoding those ids throws IllegalArgumentException, so the context this feature exists to recover is unreadable. The hot-deploy refresh in getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut (puts around lines 113 and 131) also overwrites grantsByShortcuts without re-checking length or uniqueness. Two grants that share a shortcut leave one decode mapping, so previously issued tokens of the overwritten grant are reported as the other grant type. Registration should reject anything other than a unique 2-character shortcut, and the javadoc must match that contract.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate points out that the javadoc says 'usually like 3-letters' while the format requires 2-character shortcuts, and it says the javadoc must match that contract. This is the same documentation mismatch the golden comment raises. The candidate adds validation concerns on top, but the core issue is covered.

false_positives.candidate:
New getShortcut() method has no default and aborts server startup

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is the extension point for custom grant types, and getShortcut() was added with no default implementation. DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit walks every OAuth2GrantType factory and calls getShortcut() unconditionally. A custom grant JAR compiled against the previous interface does not have that method, so the call throws AbstractMethodError during provider startup and Keycloak fails to boot. A recompiled factory that returns null also aborts startup, because the shortcut is inserted into a ConcurrentHashMap, which rejects null keys. A default method is required so existing providers keep the server up, and postInit must reject invalid shortcuts with an explicit error instead of an NPE or AbstractMethodError.

Decoder throws on unknown prefixes instead of falling back like legacy ids

getTokenContextFromTokenId returns an UNKNOWN session type, token type, and grant when the jti has no ':'. If the id contains ':' but the prefix is not exactly 6 characters, or any 2-character slice is missing from the in-memory maps, it throws IllegalArgumentException. The length error says the token id 'Expected length of 6', but the check is only on the prefix before the colon, so the message is wrong and will mislead operators. Unknown shortcuts are a normal compatibility case, not corruption: feature-gated grants are absent from the maps when that feature is disabled or not deployed on this node (CIBA 'ci', device 'dg', token-exchange 'te', pre-authorized code 'pc'), and another Keycloak version can mint shortcuts this node does not know. Introspection or session lookup that uses this method, which is the stated purpose of the encoding, will then fail a still-valid access token instead of falling back to the old online-then-offline lookup. Unsupported prefixes should return an UNKNOWN context, the same as colon-less legacy ids.

Non-standard token exchange issues access tokens with unknown grant

The encoded grant type is whatever was stored on the client-session attribute Constants.GRANT_TYPE. If that attribute is missing, DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider records 'na' (unknown). Token exchange does not go through OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse, which is why this provider had to set the attribute itself before generateAccessToken(). Only StandardTokenExchangeProvider.exchangeClientToOIDCClient was updated. TokenExchangeGrantTypeFactory still turns on legacy TOKEN_EXCHANGE, TOKEN_EXCHANGE_FEDERATED_V2, and TOKEN_EXCHANGE_SUBJECT_IMPERSONATION_V2, and those providers are not in this change. StandardTokenExchangeProvider rejects requested_subject, so impersonation cannot be this method. Those other flows still call TokenManager to mint access tokens, so their jti grant shortcut is 'na' rather than 'te'. Follow-up token-exchange logic that branches on the encoded grant (the #37117 case described in the PR) will not recognize them. The new AssertEvents matcher does not actually verify the grant shortcut, so CI will not catch this.

Replacing form params leaves the cached grant type stale

grantType is captured once in the Context constructor from formParams.getFirst(grant_type) and is what OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse writes into the client session before the access token id is encoded. setFormParams replaces formParams but does not recompute grantType, so getGrantType() can disagree with the params the grant then processes. A caller that uses the existing setter to change the request after construction will encode the original grant type into the access-token id. The constructor also now dereferences formParams, so a null map NPEs, which the previous constructor accepted. This change also removes the public Context(Context) copy constructor, so extensions that cloned a context that way no longer compile and have no other way to rebuild grantType.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
User-storage recovery codes are stored in cleartext and never consumed

updateCredential writes input.getChallengeResponse() — the JSON array of raw recovery codes from CredentialHelper — straight into credentialData (line 197). isValid deserializes that list and returns true if any entry equals the submitted code. It does not delete the matched code, mark it used, or require the next unused code. getCredentials then rebuilds the credential with RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues (line 237), which hashes the original list, marks every code unused, and does not copy the id that was stored on the saved credential. disableCredentialType (line 217) and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream (line 259) only handle OTP, so recovery codes cannot be disabled from account or admin APIs. Local recovery codes are hashed and one-time; this provider keeps plaintext codes valid for the life of the server-side user map, the login form always asks for code 0, and the authenticator's all-codes-used branch is unreachable. testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only submits the first code once, so it passes even though the same code can be replayed.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate's main focus is on plaintext storage and codes never being consumed. It does, however, explicitly say that getCredentials rebuilds the credential with createFromValues and "does not copy the id that was stored on the saved credential." That is the same defect the golden comment describes. The candidate does not spell out the downstream removal-by-id consequence, but it is closely related to its point about codes never being consumed.

false_positives.candidate:
Rotating recovery codes into user storage leaves old local codes valid

createRecoveryCodesCredential treats a true result from user.credentialManager().updateCredential as done and returns without deleting recovery-authn-codes credentials already stored in Keycloak's local database. The local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential path is skipped in that branch, and nothing else removes those rows. Federated users who already had recovery codes locally (the only option before their user-storage provider accepted this type, or if another API wrote them locally) and then regenerate will keep the old set. UserCredentialManager.isValid accepts a code if any supporting CredentialInputValidator accepts it, and the local recovery-code provider validates local credentials independently of user storage, so the retired codes still authenticate after rotation. RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential also prefers the federated credential, so the login form can show the new code number while the old codes still work. The same gap exists in the other direction: if updateCredential returns false but user storage already holds codes, the fallback local create adds a second valid set and does not disable the user-storage one. After a successful user-storage write the helper must remove existing local recovery-authn-codes credentials, and when falling back to local storage it must disable the user-storage credential, so only one set remains valid.

Spent federated recovery codes are not removed and the next login crashes

After a recovery code is accepted, the authenticator reloads the credential through RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential, which now returns a user-storage credential ahead of a local one. If that model reports all codes used, it calls credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById. That API only deletes credentials in Keycloak's local credential store; a federated credential id is not there, so the call is a no-op and the user-storage credential stays configured. isConfiguredFor therefore remains true. CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES is added, but required actions run only after the browser flow succeeds. On the next login the recovery-code authenticator still runs and constructs RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean, which unconditionally calls getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get() (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean.java line 21). With no unused code left that throws NoSuchElementException, the user gets an error page, and never reaches the setup action. If the browser flow requires recovery codes, they cannot sign in. Spent federated credentials have to be removed through the user-storage disable path (disableCredentialType or an equivalent federated remove), not only removeStoredCredentialById. BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.disableCredentialType (line 217) currently ignores recovery-authn-codes, so that provider must clear them as well or this path cannot be fixed end to end.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

false_positives.candidate:
Default update-strategy tests never enable rolling-updates

createInitialDeployment returns immediately when the update strategy is null, and the new code that sets spec.features.enabled to rolling-updates runs only for a non-null strategy. The parameterized image-change and cache-max-count tests call this helper with both null (the default strategy) and Recreate. The operator guide in this PR says that while the feature is preview it must be enabled or the operator fails, including for the default strategy that still decides rolling vs recreate on image changes. The default-strategy cases therefore never put rolling-updates on the Keycloak CR, which is the configuration users are told to set. Those tests either fail when the compatibility command rejects a feature-disabled server, or they pass only because operator/scripts/Dockerfile-custom-image now bakes the feature into the test image and never cover the documented CR path. Enable the feature for every deployment this helper builds, before the null return. setEnabledFeatures(List.of(...)) also replaces any features already on the CR instead of appending rolling-updates, so a deployment that already enables features loses them in the Recreate cases.

Exit code 4 changed meaning from recreate to feature-disabled

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE was 4 and is now 3, and 4 is reused as FEATURE_DISABLED. The update-compatibility check exit code is the public contract the guide tells automation to branch on. After this change an incompatible deployment exits 3 instead of 4, and exit 4 means the preview feature is off and no compatibility decision was made. Callers that observed the previous implementation (exit 4 = shut the deployment down and recreate) will treat a disabled feature as recreate-required, and will not treat a real incompatibility (now exit 3) as recreate-required, which can allow a rolling update the tool rejected or cause a full shutdown when the user only needed to enable the feature. The guide already listed 3 for recreate before this PR, so the old constant disagreed with the guide; if that text is the shipped contract, aligning the constant is right, but nothing in this PR updates operator production code that may still compare the job status to a literal 4. UpdateCommandDistTest does not assert either code, so CI will not catch a regression to the old value.

New and renumbered compatibility exit codes are not asserted

The distribution tests never check the exit codes this PR defines. testFeatureNotEnabled only asserts that stderr contains the disabled-feature message, and it only launches the metadata subcommand; it does not assert exit code 4, and there is no equivalent case for check. testWrongVersions only asserts the incompatibility error text after RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE moved from 4 to 3, so a build that still exits 4 (now the feature-disabled code) would still pass. The guide tells automation to branch on these codes (0 rolling, 3 recreate, 4 feature disabled). Assert the process exit code for both subcommands when rolling-updates is off, and assert exit code 3 when the stored versions are incompatible.

Documented --features flag replaces other enabled features

The updatecompatibility doc macro now renders every example as bin/kc.sh update-compatibility <args> --features=rolling-updates. Keycloak gives CLI arguments precedence over KC_FEATURES and keycloak.conf, and features is a single list-valued option, not a set merged across sources. Copying the documented command therefore replaces any other explicitly enabled features with only rolling-updates. The same guide says every option from the real deployment must be present and that omitting options produces an incorrect rolling-versus-recreate outcome. The examples should tell users to add rolling-updates to their existing enabled-feature list rather than hard-coding a replacement --features value.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
V2 client grants are not removed when the client is deleted

Per-client FGAP resources are named with the client id and are not foreign-keyed to the client, so deleting the client does not cascade them. The only hook added here is the ClientRemovedEvent listener, and the new feature gate skips that hook unless ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is enabled. In the V2-only setup this work targets, client deletion leaves the admin-permissions resource and its scope permissions in place. Listings keep a grant for a client that no longer exists, and getResourceName returns null for it. setPermissionsEnabled cannot be used to clean this up because the V2 implementation throws.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. The cleanup listener is gated on the V1 flag, so with only V2 enabled, deleting a client leaves orphaned permissions behind. The candidate focuses on client removal specifically, but the root cause is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
All-clients permission is returned as the id Clients

getClientsWithPermission adds resource.getName() for every Clients-typed resource whose evaluation grants the scope. The schema resource created for "all clients" is named Clients and has that type, so a type-level grant puts the literal string Clients into the set. That is not a client UUID. Callers that keep clients where granted.contains(client.getId()) will not treat the grant as access to every client, and nothing expands the type resource into real client ids. There is no global canMapRoles() to compensate, so an all-clients map-roles or view permission does not show those clients in filters that rely on this method.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that getClientsWithPermission iterates type-level Clients resources and returns resource.getName() ('Clients'), which is not an actual client ID, so callers expecting client IDs behave incorrectly. Same core issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Null all-clients resource NPEs permission checks

If no per-client resource exists, hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) loads the type resource with getResourceTypeResource and immediately calls PolicyStore.findByResource(server, resource). getResourceTypeResource returns null when the Clients resource was never created, was deleted, or the schema is not supported for that server (admin permissions disabled while the admin-permissions client pointer remains). findByResource dereferences the resource, so the call throws NullPointerException. The no-argument hasPermission null-checks its lookup; this overload does not. View, manage, configure, and map-roles checks that reach this fallback then 500 instead of denying, for any caller who did not already pass an admin-role short-circuit.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: in hasPermission, getResourceTypeResource can return null, and passing that null to findByResource throws a NullPointerException. Both call for a null check.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Runtime client permission methods throw instead of deciding

Turning on ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 makes ClientPermissionsV2 the client evaluator for every realm, not only realms that opted into admin permissions. canExchangeTo, isPermissionsEnabled, and getPermissions unconditionally throw UnsupportedOperationException. canExchangeTo is the token-exchange authorization check (authorized client plus subject token) and used to return a boolean, including role-based allow or deny; a throw is a 500, not a deny. isPermissionsEnabled and getPermissions are still the client management-permissions API and are reachable from any parent method that was not overridden, so those calls 500 as well. Unimplemented V2 behavior needs to fail closed or keep the manage-clients role path, not throw. getEvaluationContext in this class is unused, so the exchange path was left unfinished.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate's main issue is the methods that throw UnsupportedOperationException. It does also say getEvaluationContext is unused, which is the golden's point, but only as supporting evidence and not as the core issue. That is a partial match.

false_positives.candidate:
Role-mapping checks drop manage-clients and master admins

canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission. They never short-circuit on root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS), unlike canManage(ClientModel). hasPermission then returns false immediately when the caller is not in the same realm. ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 installs MgmtPermissionsV2 for every realm, so this replaces the V1 evaluator: realm admins with manage-clients, and master-realm admins, can no longer map client roles, add composites, or map client-scope roles unless a fine-grained permission also grants it. V1 kept that role check inside its permission helper before any same-realm test. The new tests only use myadmin with no admin role, so they do not catch the regression. map-roles-client-scope has no test at all.

Existing admin-permissions clients never get the Clients schema

init returns as soon as realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null, and nothing in this change syncs an already created resource server. The Clients resource and the new scopes configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite are only inserted when that client is first created. Realms that already enabled fine-grained admin permissions for Users keep the old server: the Clients resource is missing and getScope fails with "Scope [configure] does not exist" (and the same for the other new scope names) when a client permission is created. Evaluation then falls through to a null type resource and can 500. Only freshly initialized realms work.

Client deletion throws when both FGAP features are enabled

The removal listener is gated on ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ, but AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, even if the V1 feature is also on. ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled always throws UnsupportedOperationException. With both features enabled, ClientRemovedEvent calls that method and the exception propagates from the provider listener, failing or rolling back client deletion. Role and group removal still use the V1 evaluators, so only clients are broken. The listener must not call the V2 implementation, or setPermissionsEnabled must be a no-op under V2.

Client resources are returned with a null display name

getResourceName only special-cases Users: the type resource becomes "All users" and other names are resolved to usernames, throwing ModelIllegalStateException if the user is gone. Client resources are stored under the internal client id (resolveClient returns client.getId()) and are created without a display name, so they hit return resource.getDisplayName() and come back null. The all-clients resource is named Clients and is not labeled "All clients". Permission listings for the new type show blank names, and a deleted client does not surface the missing-object error used for users.

Client tests rotate myclient's secret and do not restore it

testConfigureOnlyOneClient calls generateNewSecret and invalidateRotatedSecret on myclient and never puts the original secret back. realmAdminClient is injected for the class as client myclient; the sibling impersonation helper logs in with client secret mysecret. After rotation, refresh for that confidential client fails, so later methods in this class can 401 once the access token is no longer reused. testManageOnlyOneClient also renames myclient and removeDefaultClientScope without restoring either, and AfterEach only deletes scope permissions, so later methods share that leaked client state.

requireView javadoc says a void method returns true

The new javadoc on requireView says it returns true if canView() returns true, but the method is void and throws ForbiddenException when the check fails, same as requireManage. requireViewClientScopes (line 102) has the same error: it says it returns true if canViewClientScopes() returns true. Implementors reading only the contract will treat these as predicates instead of enforcing checks.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Groups VIEW scope is treated as manage

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() passes both VIEW and MANAGE to hasPermission and returns true if either scope is granted. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup authorizes only with requireManage(), so an admin who was granted view-only on groups can create top-level groups and can move an existing group to the top of the tree by posting its id. canManage(GroupModel) correctly requires MANAGE, and UserPermissions.canManage() does not treat view as manage. The new GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage() javadoc repeats this incorrect contract and should be corrected with the implementation.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug as the golden comment. GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() checks both the VIEW and MANAGE scopes, so users with only VIEW permission pass the manage check.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Member-view filter stores authorization resource ids, not group ids

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() is the set UsersResource.getUsersCount, UsersResource.searchForUser, and BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser apply as the groups whose members the caller may see. The findByType callback passes groupResource.getId() (the authorization resource primary key) both into hasPermission() and into the returned set. hasPermission() looks up resources by name, and per-group resources are named with the group id, so the lookup misses the group, falls back to the all-groups resource, and ignores the per-group view-members/manage-members grant. The ids placed in the session UserModel.GROUPS attribute are not group ids, and the schema resource named "Groups" is itself included by findByType. User search then matches nobody, so paginated results omit users the admin is allowed to see; when the set is empty, the query is not constrained and getUsersCount returns 0 while the list path only filters later in memory. GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest only calls users().search and never checks counts, so it does not catch this.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug. getGroupIdsWithViewPermission passes and stores groupResource.getId(), which is a resource id, while hasPermission resolves by name, i.e. by group id. Both note this breaks per-group permission evaluation, causes a fallback to the all-groups resource, and produces wrong ids for UserModel.GROUPS and the count filters.

false_positives.candidate:
Per-group authz resources are created without a type

getOrCreateResource() creates the per-object resource and updates scopes, but never calls setType(resourceType). V1 GroupPermissions.initialize did set the type. GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() discovers groups with resourceStore.findByType(server, "Groups"), so individual group resources are invisible to that scan and view-members/manage-members grants never contribute real group ids to the user-search filter. Only the schema-level resource created in init(), which does set type, is found. Because the type is also unset, an evaluator that applies resource-type policies only to typed resources will not apply all-groups policies to these rows either.

Group deletion hits unsupported V2 setPermissionsEnabled

AdminPermissions.registerListener still handles every GroupRemovedEvent by calling management().groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled. With ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 also enabled, groups() is now GroupPermissionsV2, and setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException. The listener is invoked from realm.removeGroup with no catch, so deleting any group (not only groups that have permissions) fails with a 500 and rolls back. V1 fine-grained admin authz is commonly enabled together with V2. If only V2 is enabled, the listener is not registered at all because it checks the V1 feature, so authorization resources created for a group by getOrCreateResource are never removed when the group is deleted. The same throw breaks the V1 management/permissions admin endpoint, which calls setPermissionsEnabled after requiring ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ.

All-groups policies are skipped once a per-group resource exists

hasPermission() evaluates only the per-group resource when findByName finds one, and loads the Groups type resource only when that lookup returns null. getOrCreateResource creates that row as soon as any permission references the group, including a different admin or a different scope such as view-members. After that, GroupPermissionsV2 never consults all-groups allow or deny policies for that group: an admin with all-groups MANAGE loses update, delete, and membership checks on it, and a negative all-groups policy does not deny a scope granted by the specific resource. Group listing no longer short-circuits on canView(), so those groups also disappear from an admin who only has all-groups view. testManageAllGroups only updates a group that has no specific resource, so only the fallback path is tested.

Existing admin-permissions clients never receive the Groups schema

init() returns immediately when the realm already has an admin-permissions client, so upgrade does not add the Groups resource type, the "Groups" all-resource, or the new scopes manage-membership, manage-members, and view-members. On those realms, creating a group permission fails: getScope throws ModelValidationException because the scope does not exist, and getOrCreateResource throws ModelException ("No scopes found") when attaching scopes. GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission then gets a null type resource from getResourceTypeResource and passes it to policyStore.findByResource and resource.getScopes(), which are not null-safe, so group list and permission checks for fine-grained admins throw NullPointerException instead of denying. This pull request contains no migration.

Scope grants are accepted without matching the evaluated resource

After evaluatePermission, GroupPermissionsV2 returns true for any permission whose scopes intersect the requested scopes. UserPermissionsV2, which this evaluator copies, ignores permissions whose resource id is not the resource just evaluated, because the result is not guaranteed to contain only that resource. Omitting the check here can apply a scope granted on another resource to the group being checked, widening view, manage, view-members, manage-members, or manage-membership beyond that group's policies.

Group list runs a policy evaluation per group

V2 canView(GroupModel) does not reuse the no-arg canView() result, and GroupsResource.getGroups and GroupResource.getSubGroups dropped the previous canViewGlobal short-circuit. An admin whose access comes from an all-groups permission therefore runs a full authorization evaluation for every group on the page, even though each call falls back to the same Groups type resource. On realms with large group trees the groups admin API issues one policy evaluation, and several store queries, per group on every list request.

Group permission resources have no resolvable name

getResourceName() maps Users resources to the username, but a Groups resource falls through to resource.getDisplayName(). getOrCreateResource() stores the group id as the resource name and never sets a display name, so the authorization admin API shows a null name, or a raw id, for group permissions instead of the group name. After the group is deleted or renamed those resources stay unresolved, whereas a missing user at least throws ModelIllegalStateException.

requireManageMembers javadoc cites the wrong method

The javadoc on requireManageMembers says it throws ForbiddenException if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false. The implementation throws when canManageMembers returns false. Those are different scopes (manage-membership versus manage-members), so the published contract on this permission interface is wrong.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider

CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider is specified to return the BouncyCastle or BCFIPS Provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is whichever JDK provider implements the default keystore type (typically SUN, or SunJSSE when the default type is PKCS12) and follows the keystore.type security property. Callers that pass this Provider into Signature.getInstance, Cipher.getInstance, or CertificateFactory.getInstance do not get BouncyCastle algorithms. PKCS7 padding, BCFKS, and other BC-only operations fail, or they silently run on a non-FIPS JDK provider. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null for this method and callers already null-check and fall back; a non-null SUN provider skips that fallback. This should return null or throw UnsupportedOperationException like the other unimplemented methods, not an unrelated JCA provider.
true_positives.reasoning: Both say getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider instead of BouncyCastle. Same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() is abstract, so existing CryptoProvider implementations crash

CryptoProvider is a public SPI implemented outside this interface (the default, Elytron, and FIPS artifacts, plus downstream crypto providers). order() was added as an abstract method with no default. An implementation compiled against the previous interface throws AbstractMethodError when ServiceLoader instantiates it and detectProvider sorts with CryptoProvider::order. That error aborts provider detection entirely, so Keycloak will not start even if a newer provider on the classpath would have been selected. A default method returning a low value (below AuthzClientCryptoProvider's 100 and the in-tree providers' 200) would keep existing implementations loadable and still prefer the updated providers.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same issue: order() was added to the CryptoProvider SPI as an abstract method, which breaks existing implementations and so breaks backward compatibility. The candidate adds detail on the AbstractMethodError and suggests a default method.

false_positives.candidate:
Tied crypto providers are chosen silently instead of failing startup

detectProvider used to throw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath, which stopped the server from running with an ambiguous crypto stack. It now sorts by CryptoProvider.order() descending and always returns the first entry, logging the rest only at debug. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so they tie. Stream.sorted is stable, so the winner is whichever jar ServiceLoader encounters first (classpath or module order), not an explicit preference. A deployment that accidentally contains both the default BouncyCastle provider and the FIPS provider — previously a startup error — will now boot and can run non-FIPS crypto, or drop Elytron in favor of BC, with no error and no info-level log. ServiceLoader also instantiates every provider before the sort, so the losing provider's constructor still registers JCA providers and mutates security properties, and the process continues in that mixed state. AuthzClientCryptoProvider at order 100 is correctly deprioritized, but that does not require ignoring a tie at the winning order. If several providers share the maximum order, startup should still fail and list them. Nothing in this change tests that selection.

AuthzClient.create permanently pins CryptoIntegration to its classloader

CryptoIntegration.init is process-global and returns immediately once a provider is set, so the first caller permanently chooses it. AuthzClient.create now calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) as a side effect of constructing a client. ServiceLoader therefore runs only against that classloader, not the thread context classloader and not the classloader a later server or application init would pass. If this runs first in a JVM where AuthzClient's classloader can see AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100) but not DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, or WildFlyElytronProvider — for example keycloak-common in a parent classloader and the real crypto module only in a child — the stub provider is installed and every later CryptoIntegration.init is a no-op. PEM, signature, certificate, AES, and truststore calls then throw UnsupportedOperationException, and the server no longer uses BouncyCastle or FIPS. Before this change, creating an AuthzClient did not initialize crypto, so the server's own init still selected the intended provider. A library constructor should not freeze detection, or a later init that finds a higher-order provider must be allowed to replace the stub.

ECDSA test never checks JCA DER or the real curve sizes

ECDSAAlgorithmTest builds one KeyPair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() and no ECGenParameterSpec, so the key is the JVM default curve (P-256 on SunEC). It then runs ES256, ES384, and ES512 against that same key and only asserts that asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(rs)) equals rs. It never checks that the DER matches the original Signature.sign() bytes, and it never calls Signature.verify on the converted DER. A codec that is self-inverse but not valid DER still passes, and integerToBytes silently pads or truncates to algorithm.getSignatureLength(), so a P-256 signature padded out to the ES512 length of 132 also round-trips. Because R and S stay about 32 bytes, sequence and integer lengths stay under 128, so the long-form length paths in ASN1Encoder.writeLength and ASN1Decoder.readLength — required for real P-521 signatures — are never executed. Provider ordering is also untested. The test should initialize secp256r1, secp384r1, and secp521r1 explicitly, assert the DER equals the JCA signature or verifies, and cover ServiceLoader selection.

When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

The previous code called getGroupModel() directly, so a missing row was not stuck on the adapter. After a concurrent delete the cache can still hand out this GroupAdapter while the database lookup returns null; the first count call then pins modelSupplier to null for the rest of the session. true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.

createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti starts a non-daemon Thread at line 139 that lists groups until deletedAll is true, but the test never retains that Thread, never joins it, and never sets deletedAll in a finally block. After the deletes it sets deletedAll (line 155) and immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty (line 157). There is also no start latch and no check that a read ran during the deletes, so an empty list does not prove the bug was exercised. If any group remove() throws, deletedAll stays false and the non-daemon reader loops forever, which keeps the Surefire JVM alive and can hang the suite. Even on the success path the in-flight HTTP call continues after the test method returns and races with later tests that share this class's injected realm and admin client. true_positives.reasoning: The candidate makes the same point as the golden comment. The reader thread is never joined, and deletedAll is set right before the assertion runs. Exceptions added after the flag flip can therefore be missed, which makes the test unreliable.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative cursor offsets crash queryset slicing

When enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset < 0, OptimizedCursorPaginator slices with queryset[cursor.offset:stop]. Django querysets do not support negative indexes and raise ValueError or AssertionError ("Negative indexing is not supported."). Endpoint.paginate only maps BadPaginationError to HTTP 400, so a client-supplied cursor such as value:-5:0 becomes a 500. The audit-log endpoint always passes enable_advanced_features=True on this path, and Cursor.from_string accepts any integer offset with no lower bound. The comments that the ORM handles negative slices and that this safely reaches data beyond pagination bounds because permissions are checked on the queryset are wrong: a negative slice does not succeed, and slicing would not remove the queryset WHERE clause anyway. Reject offset < 0 with BadPaginationError, as OffsetPaginator already does.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug as the golden comment. OptimizedCursorPaginator slices the queryset with a negative offset, which Django does not support, so it raises an AssertionError or ValueError.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.

That RPC object has no has_global_access attribute (global access is derived from member.role via organization roles), and member is None for some callers that still pass OrganizationAuditPermission, such as org-auth tokens. Any non-superuser therefore raises AttributeError and the previously working audit-log endpoint returns 500 even when optimized_pagination is absent and the DateTimePaginator path would have run. Superusers only avoid this because is_superuser short-circuits the or. Guard member is not None and check the role (organization_roles.get(member.role).is_global) only inside the new branch.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly notes that member is None for org-auth tokens and that accessing has_global_access then raises an AttributeError. That is the golden issue. It also adds further claims, such as the attribute not existing at all and the check running on every GET, but these do not change the fact that it identifies the same bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Optimized paginator cannot order audit logs by datetime

The new branch paginates AuditLogEntry with OptimizedCursorPaginator and order_by="-datetime". That class implements get_item_key with math.floor/math.ceil on the order field and value_from_cursor by returning the raw cursor number (paginator.py around lines 839-843), which is the numeric Paginator contract, not DateTimePaginator. AuditLogEntry.datetime is a datetime, so any non-empty page raises TypeError while build_cursor computes next/prev keys. A later request that supplies a cursor also fails in SQL: build_queryset compares the timestamp column to that integer/float cursor value instead of converting with DateTimePaginator's millisecond multiplier and datetime.fromtimestamp. The optimized path cannot return a successful page or a usable Link cursor. It needs DateTimePaginator key handling (or should not replace DateTimePaginator).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate makes the same point as the golden comment. OptimizedCursorPaginator's get_item_key calls math.floor/ceil on the datetime order field when paginating audit logs by -datetime, and this raises a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared paginator silently rewrites negative forward offsets

BasePaginator.get_result backs every Paginator and DateTimePaginator list endpoint, including the unchanged audit-log path. The new start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset changes results for a forward cursor whose offset is negative. The cursor query param is client-controlled. Previously that slice failed; now the offset is forced to 0 and a page is returned, which repeats rows at that cursor value instead of rejecting the cursor. Previous-page cursors still pass a negative offset straight into the queryset slice, so those requests 500, despite the new comment saying negative offsets are a safe optimization the queryset will handle. This is not a performance improvement for valid cursors (non-negative offsets behave exactly as before). Invalid offsets should raise BadPaginationError in both directions, and this global change should be reverted.

No tests for the new paginator or offset behavior

The PR adds OptimizedCursorPaginator, switches organization audit logs onto it behind optimized_pagination, and changes BasePaginator slicing, but adds no tests. Existing audit-log and paginator tests do not cover a non-superuser GET (which now touches member.has_global_access on every request), optimized_pagination=true with a datetime order key, cursor resume, or a negative cursor offset on either paginator. Those cases 500 or return a different page and need an endpoint test plus a paginator unit test before this can merge.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Narrowed BuildIndex lock races same-key builds and clobbers the cache

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for the entire build, which serialized bleve.New and cache publication. The mutex is now taken only for b.cache[key] = idx. getOrCreateIndex in search.go is still check-then-build with no per-key lock (the TODO above it says so), so two searches, or a search and a watch event, for a namespace that was not prebuilt can both miss the cache and build at once. File-backed builds then call bleve.New on the same directory concurrently; that races inside bleve, and the loser fails with path-already-exists even though an index was created. Memory builds both succeed and the later cache write replaces the earlier index without closing it, so watch updates applied to the replaced index disappear from later searches and the orphaned index leaks. In-flight builds need to be deduplicated per NamespacedResource, and the cache insert must keep an existing entry instead of overwriting it.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same problem. Narrowing cacheMu to cover only the cache assignment lets concurrent goroutines build the same index for the same key.

false_positives.candidate:
Parallel index init shares err and can ignore build failures

searchSupport.init starts one errgroup goroutine per namespace, but every goroutine assigns the build result to the single outer err variable and returns that same variable. BuildIndex used to hold its cache mutex for the whole build, so those goroutines mostly ran one at a time; after the lock was narrowed they actually run in parallel and the unsynchronized err writes race. A goroutine whose build failed can observe nil after another goroutine's success overwrites err, return nil, and let errgroup.Wait succeed, so the server starts with that namespace missing from the index. The reverse also happens: a successful goroutine can return another goroutine's error and fail startup incorrectly. totalBatchesIndexed is incremented from the same goroutines without synchronization. Each goroutine needs its own error variable.

Index watch starts at the latest RV and drops writes made during the build

build returns the resource version observed while listing a namespace, and the comment on that return says watchers must apply every event since that version. init discards the returned version and then calls WatchWriteEvents, which samples the latest resource version at subscription time and only delivers newer rows. Creates, updates, and deletes that commit after a namespace was listed and before that subscription — expected when another HA replica writes during the long startup index build — are neither in the listed snapshot nor replayed. Updated documents stay stale in the search index, and deletes from that window remain searchable until a full rebuild. Namespaces are listed concurrently, so each list has its own version; the watch cursor has to be the earliest of those list versions, not the global maximum after every build finishes.

File indexes cannot be reopened, so eager init fails every restart

File-backed indexes are created with bleve.New on a stable path (Root/namespace/resource.group). bleve.New fails if that directory already exists, and this code never calls bleve.Open or deletes a leftover directory. If the builder fails, BuildIndex returns without closing the index or removing the partial directory. After the first successful file-backed build, or after a failed build that created the directory, the next process calls BuildIndex again, bleve.New fails, and NewResourceServer now aborts Init and refuses to construct the server. FileThreshold's zero value is 0, so any namespace with a positive count uses disk unless the caller sets a higher threshold. Startup must reopen or replace an existing directory, and error paths must delete partial indexes, or a normal restart cannot bring the storage server up.

Init failure returns nil without rolling back partial startup

NewResourceServer now calls Init and, on error, returns nil without calling the cancel func created above, lifecycle.Stop, or closing the blob bucket opened earlier in the constructor. If lifecycle.Init already opened the SQL database, those connections leak because the caller has no server value on which to call Stop. If search indexing succeeded and only the later watcher setup failed, search.init has already started a watch goroutine on context.Background that nothing will stop. Indexes already published into the caller-owned SearchBackend stay cached, so a retry that reuses that backend treats them as complete and skips rebuilding. Failure needs to stop lifecycle hooks, cancel background work, and drop partial indexes before returning the error.

Search watch loop ignores shutdown and panics when the event channel closes

After indexing, init starts a goroutine that reads WatchWriteEvents in a bare for loop and does not check the receive ok value. The watch context is context.Background, not the server context cancelled by Stop, so server shutdown does not stop the loop. The SQL poller closes that channel when the backend stops; the next receive yields a nil event, and handleEvent immediately dereferences evt.Type and panics, crashing the process during shutdown. If the backend is never stopped, the goroutine and poller leak for the rest of the process. Init now runs inside NewResourceServer, so this goroutine is created for every search-enabled server, including ones that are constructed and shut down without serving a request. The loop should use the server lifetime context and exit when the channel closes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

failure_issue_threshold does not require N consecutive failures

try_incident_threshold is what opens a monitor incident after failure_issue_threshold consecutive failures. The threshold==1 path correctly uses only the current failed check-in. For any larger threshold it loads at most that many latest check-ins of any status and returns without opening an incident only if one of them is CheckInStatus.OK. An in-progress check-in in the window counts as one of the N slots the same way, so a single real failure can both pass this gate and be published as a failure occurrence. true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.queued is fixed at import time

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.

Outbound assignee task payload embeds a raw datetime

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts that commits must not happen

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says a processing error must not block commits for later messages, but the assertion requires that nothing was committed. The worker always complete_offset()s in a finally block, even when the patched processor raises, so a working consumer will commit both offsets (factory commit value 102). The wait loop returns as soon as the queue is empty, usually well under a second, while the commit thread waits 1s before its first commit. The assertion therefore passes only when the commit has not happened yet, and fails when the commit lands within the ~2s loop. It does not lock in the behavior the docstring describes, and nothing in the new tests closes a strategy and creates another one, so the rebalance data-loss path is untested.

false_positives.candidate:
Rebalance kills the shared pool, then commits unprocessed messages

FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy, but close(), terminate(), and join() all call queue_pool.shutdown(). Arroyo handles revocation by close()+join() on the current strategy, then create_with_partitions() on the same factory. shutdown() sets each worker's shutdown flag and calls Queue.shutdown(), after which put() raises queue.ShutDown. The next strategy still uses that dead pool, so every submit fails to enqueue. submit()'s except block treats that failure as success: it add_offset/complete_offset and returns, and the new commit thread then commits those offsets (the factory wrapper adds 1, so the group offset moves past them). Results already sitting in the queue at revoke are abandoned and, on redelivery, dropped the same way. After the first rebalance, scale-in, or deploy, uptime results are never handled and will not be retried for the rest of the process. Give each assignment its own pool created in create_with_partitions, and only shut it down after that assignment has drained and committed; do not destroy a factory-owned pool from close(). Tests never close a strategy and call create_with_partitions again, so they miss this.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure

Each worker queue is created with queue.Queue() (maxsize 0, unbounded) and FixedQueuePool.submit() always put()s without blocking. poll() only records a gauge. The strategy docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever blocks the consumer thread. One slow subscription occupies its single worker while the consumer keeps reading that partition into memory; WorkItem also retains the full Kafka message, which the worker never reads. Commits stop at the oldest incomplete offset, so a stuck item also prevents committing every later message on the partition and those payloads cannot be released. Because poll() keeps returning, max.poll.interval is not exceeded and Kafka will not move the partition to a healthy consumer. The process can OOM and, on crash, must reprocess the entire uncommitted backlog. Bound the queues and block in submit() or poll() when a queue is full so the consumer actually applies backpressure.

Commit callback runs off the processing thread

_commit_loop is a daemon thread started from SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__ and calls the Arroyo commit callback every second while the processor thread is in consumer.poll() and strategy.submit(). librdkafka consumers are not thread-safe, and Arroyo expects commit to run on the processing thread; concurrent staging/commit and poll can drop offset updates or fault the consumer. close() also joins this thread before workers finish, so the last snapshot misses offsets that complete during shutdown and those messages are redelivered. Commit contiguous offsets from poll() on the processing thread, and do one final commit at the end of join() after queued work is idle, instead of using a side thread.

Shutdown does not drain queues and ignores join timeout

OrderedQueueWorker leaves its loop as soon as self.shutdown is true, and FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets that flag before Queue.shutdown(immediate=False). A worker blocked in get() processes at most one more item and then exits, so the rest of the queue is never handled. close() has already stopped the commit thread, so those offsets are not committed. join() ignores the timeout it is given, calls close(), and never raises TimeoutError, so Arroyo treats shutdown as complete and will not call terminate(). Workers are daemon threads and are joined one after another with a 5s timeout each, so 20 stuck workers block the consumer thread inside close/join for about 100 seconds (which can exceed max.poll.interval.ms) and can then be killed mid-handler when the process exits, after partial side effects and without running finally. A second close() or ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() calls Queue.shutdown() again, which raises queue.ShutDown and is logged as an error on every clean shutdown. join() should drain (or raise TimeoutError), commit, then stop workers, using one shared deadline.

Queue-pool tests race the already-running workers

test_stats_reporting asserts total_items > 0 immediately after submit, but the three workers are started in setUp and only append to a list, so they can drain all 10 items before get_stats() and fail the assertion on a fast run. test_offset_committing and test_offset_gaps_block_commits treat the first commit_event as proof that the final offset was committed. The commit loop fires about once a second and sets that event for whatever prefix is contiguous at that moment, so the assertion can observe a partial offset (for example 102, or 100 on the gap test) before the later commit updates it.

false_positives.candidate:
ZUNIONSTORE sums scores and breaks redelivery

The merge calls ZUNIONSTORE with no AGGREGATE, so Redis defaults to SUM. Members are the raw span payloads and scores are end_timestamp_precise. Kafka delivery is at-least-once: a retry ZADDs the same payload into the parent key and this script unions that key into the segment key that already holds the member. Each retry adds the timestamp again (T, 2T, 3T). The previous SUNIONSTORE path was idempotent. After the new 1000-span cap, ZPOPMIN keeps the inflated duplicates and drops spans that were ingested only once. Under the cap every member is still present, so the existing flush tests do not catch it. Pass AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN) so a retry keeps a real timestamp.

Segment keys changed from SET to ZSET with no migration

Span segment keys stay at span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id, but this write switched from SADD to ZADD, add-buffer.lua switched from SCARD/SUNIONSTORE to ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE, and _load_segment_data switched from SSCAN to ZSCAN. Redis raises WRONGTYPE when those commands hit the other type. TTL is 3600s and unflushed segments live at least until the 10s/60s flush. A rolling deploy runs both versions on the same keys, and after cutover leftover SET keys cannot be updated or scanned. process_spans then errors on every retry of that batch and can stall the partition until the key expires; flush_segments fails the same way, so those spans are never emitted. Version the key prefix or dual-handle existing sets before deploying.

Parent-redirect walk cap reduced from 10000 to 1000

The loop that follows span-buf:sr redirects used to run to 10000, with a comment that a deeper chain would not be joined onto the correct segment. It is now for i = 0, 1000 and the warning is gone. This limit is not the eviction cap: it is how many parent hops are resolved to compute set_span_id. A chain longer than 1000 spans, which the old code explicitly tolerated up to 10k and which large traces can produce when batches arrive one level at a time, stops at an intermediate parent. Those spans are merged into the wrong segment key and flushed apart from their root. Restore the previous bound unless there is a measured reason to lower it.

Over-cap eviction is silent, ignores config, and can drop the root

If the segment sorted set has more than 1000 members, ZPOPMIN deletes the lowest end_timestamp_precise scores and throws the members away. The limit is hardcoded and does not read SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (default 1001), which is now unused: the flush path that enforced it, logged the span count, and incremented spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded was removed. Dropped spans are not metered and not marked on the flushed payload, and the consumer still commits the Kafka offset, so the loss is permanent and invisible. There is also no exception for the segment span, so a root whose timestamp is among the lowest is deleted while the has-root-span flag can still be set and a partial segment is emitted as a normal one. Equal scores, which the tests all use, make ZPOPMIN break ties by raw payload bytes, so which spans survive is arbitrary. Pass max_segment_spans into the script, record a metric and a truncation marker, and do not evict the segment span.

No coverage for eviction, score order, or duplicate ingest

The insert-time cap is the point of this change, but every buffer test still inserts four spans that share end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0 and only checks flushed span ids. Those assertions still pass if ZPOPMIN never runs, if it drops the wrong members, if a second process_spans of the same payloads inflates ZUNIONSTORE scores, or if a segment larger than 1000 spans is returned in full. Add a case with more than 1000 distinctly scored spans (lowest scores removed, segment span kept) and a case that processes the same payloads twice.

Buffer glossary still calls segment keys complete sets

The glossary still says span-buf:s:* keys are Redis sets containing every span payload for a segment. They are now sorted sets written with ZADD and read with ZSCAN, and ZPOPMIN drops payloads once a segment exceeds 1000 spans, so the key is neither a set nor a complete segment. The algorithm notes above still describe merging sets and never mention eviction. Following the docstring leads operators to set commands (WRONGTYPE) and to treat a flushed segment as complete.

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` runs on every `store_event` and, when `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` is truthy, overwrites `normalized_data["sample_rate"]` with that raw rate. It never sets `sample_weight` and never stores `1/client_sample_rate`. The new stats test saves `client_sample_rate: 0.1` and expects `count == 10`, while `upsampled_count` in discover.py aggregates `sum(sample_weight)`. Nothing in this PR connects those: production ingest is unchanged, and this hook does not invert the rate. Unless an out-of-diff pipeline already materializes `sample_weight` as `1/sample_rate` from the event `sample_rate` field, allowlisted `count()` queries error on an unknown column or return a non-upsampled value, and the new snuba test cannot pass. It does still mention that the hook "ignores a falsy rate via `if client_sample_rate`", which is the golden issue of 0.0 being skipped. That mention is brief but correctly identifies the problem.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

Upsampling uses the outer dataset and request query, not the query executed

`_get_event_stats` decides upsampling by calling `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` with the closed-over `dataset` and `request`, ignoring the `scoped_dataset` and `query` arguments it actually runs. Dashboard discover-split rewrites those arguments: error probes use discover and `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction`, transaction probes add `event.type:transaction`, and the outer dataset is often metrics-enhanced performance, which `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` always rejects. The helper only looks at `request.GET["query"]`, so every probe inherits the original request's decision. A transaction probe whose original query contains `event.type:error` is still rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)` and comes back empty or errors; `check_if_results_have_data` then reports no transactions and `save_split_decision` persists that on `DashboardWidget.discover_widget_split`. Later loads skip the check and keep the wrong split. Error-only split queries whose original request text did not contain `event.type:error` are never upsampled. Pass the executed dataset and query string into the check. The outer `except Exception` retry calls `_get_event_stats` again, so a Snuba failure from the rewrite is not avoided and surfaces as a 500 (the endpoint only catches `ValidationError`).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: the upsampling check uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset. It also notes that dashboard split runs against discover while the outer dataset is metrics, which causes upsampling to be skipped. It adds extra detail about the query string, but the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Upsampled count drops events with no weight and truncates

`upsampled_count` is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`, and the helper comment says null checks are intentionally omitted. ClickHouse `sum` skips NULLs, so any error in an allowlisted project that has no `sample_weight` (historical events, events ingested before the column was filled, or unsampled events that should count as 1) contributes nothing. Enabling the allowlist can therefore make the series smaller than raw `count()`, including showing 0. `toInt64` truncates toward zero, so a fractional weight such as `1/0.3` is biased low on every bucket (one event at 3.333 becomes 3). If `sample_weight` is actually the rate 0.1 rather than the multiplier 10, `toInt64(sum(...))` is 0, not the 10 the new test expects. The aggregate needs a missing-weight default of 1 and rounding (for example `round(sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1)))`). With that default, mixed queries would not need the all-or-nothing allowlist gate, which today changes a project's displayed count depending on whether every other selected project is allowlisted.

Error-query check is a substring match and false-positives on negation

`_is_error_focused_query` lowercases `request.GET["query"]` and returns true when the substring `event.type:error` appears anywhere. That is true for `!event.type:error`, for `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, and for a quoted value such as `message:"event.type:error"`. On an allowlisted project set those queries rewrite `count()` to `sum(sample_weight)`. Non-error rows do not have a usable weight, so the stats request undercounts (NULLs add nothing) or fails in Snuba. The same check misses the usual discover error filter `!event.type:transaction` and list syntax such as `event.type:[error]`, so those error queries stay at the raw sampled count. The unit tests only cover the exact strings `event.type:error` and `event.type:transaction`, so the negation false positive is untested. Parse the search query and honor negation instead of substring matching.

Top-events ranking, equations, and count filters are not upsampled

Only the y-axis list is rewritten, and `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` replaces a column only when the entire string is `count()` after strip and lower. `top_events_timeseries` still gets `selected_columns` from `get_field_list`, `equations` from `get_equation_list`, and `orderby` from `get_orderby`, plus the raw `user_query`. Top-N is therefore ranked by sampled `count()` while the series uses `upsampled_count() as count`, so a heavily sampled group can be dropped from the top N, and an orderby that still names `count()` can fail the query because that aggregate was renamed. Aggregate conditions such as `count():>10` in the user query stay raw. Equation y-axes (`equation|count() / count_unique(user)`), `count() as <alias>`, `epm()`, and `eps()` are not rewritten either, so one response can mix upsampled and sampled series. Rewrite every count-based aggregate the query will run, or refuse those shapes while upsampling is on.

Allowlist cache is slower than options.get and cannot be invalidated

Every organization events-stats request now does a default-cache get (Redis in production) under `error_upsampling_eligible:{org}:{hash(sorted(project_ids))}`, and a set on miss, to avoid `options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist")`. That option read is already process-local memory, so this adds a network round trip and a high-cardinality key (one entry per distinct project-id set) on a hot endpoint. The cached boolean does not include the allowlist version. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called, and it can delete only one project-set key, so an allowlist edit cannot drop the other combinations. For up to 60 seconds after a project is removed, stats keep rewriting `count()` to `sum(sample_weight)` and can 500 or return weighted counts for projects that are no longer eligible; after a project is added, counts stay raw. The note on `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` says the allowlist is read fresh on every call so config changes apply immediately, which is false once this cache is in front. Read the option directly, or cache it in-process keyed by the allowlist contents and actually invalidate it.

upsampled_count is public, so the allowlist does not gate the feature

The new `SnQLFunction` is registered without `private=True`, unlike the internal aggregate immediately above it. The allowlist logic only rewrites a y-axis that is exactly `count()`; it does not block callers from requesting the function themselves. Any client can pass `yAxis=upsampled_count()` on discover and bypass the rollout. On datasets or projects where `sample_weight` is absent (transactions, spans, non-allowlisted projects) that same public function turns a user-controlled y-axis into a failed stats query. The aggregate should stay internal to the rewrite path so the allowlist is actually what enables it.

errors dataset always rewrites count() but the function is only added on discover

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns true for any `sentry.snuba.errors` query, and the endpoint then sends `upsampled_count()` to that dataset's query builder. The aggregate is only inserted into discover.py's `function_converter`. `sentry.search.events.builder.errors` is not changed, and `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest` never passes `dataset=errors` (it uses the default dataset plus `query=event.type:error`). If the errors dataset does not inherit Discover's function map, every allowlisted `dataset=errors` stats request fails with an unknown function as soon as the allowlist is non-empty. The string-level unit test does not run the query builder, so it would not catch that. Register the function on the errors dataset config and add a snuba test that uses `dataset=errors`.

Upsampling stats tests share one cache key and disagree on the allowlist

These tests patch `sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options` but not `sentry.utils.cache.cache`. Eligibility is cached for 60 seconds under a key built only from organization id and the project id set. All four tests use the same projects, so they share that key, while stubbing three different allowlists (both ids, one id, and empty) and expecting different counts (10 vs 1). This class's `setUp` never calls `cache.clear()` or deletes that key, and Django's `TestCase` does not clear the cache. If an earlier test cached true, `test_error_upsampling_with_partial_allowlist` and `test_error_upsampling_with_no_allowlisted_projects` still rewrite `count()` and their `count == 1` assertions fail; the reverse order makes the allowlisted test expect 10 and get 1. Mock or clear the cache in `setUp`.

Transaction upsampling test queries before the event is ingested

`test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events` calls `store_event` for a transaction and immediately GETs events-stats. `setUp` has to call `wait_for_event_count` before its queries, so ingestion is asynchronous here. The assertion that the first bucket `count` is 1 races the consumer and flakes at 0. Waiting for `wait_for_event_count(self.project.id, 1)` would also be wrong: `setUp` already stored an error in that project, so a count of 1 is satisfied before the transaction is written. Wait until that transaction is actually queryable (for example project event count 2, or a transaction-specific query) before asserting.

This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key collides for UIDs that contain underscores

userPermDenialCacheKey joins name and parent with '_' (namespace.perm_<user>_<action>_<name>_<parent>). Dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, and those two fields sit next to each other, so different pairs encode to the same key. For example name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both end in _a_b_c for the same user and action. The cache only stores negatives, so a deny for one resource is returned for the other for 30s without checking permissions, and a user who can access one of them is incorrectly denied. Use an unambiguous encoding (length prefixes, a delimiter that cannot appear in UIDs, or a hash).

false_positives.candidate:
Negative checks reload full permissions from the DB per resource

Check only returns early when the cached permission set allows the request (line 131). Any cache hit that does not allow, and any cache miss, falls through to getIdentityPermissions, and the in-function cache read was removed from getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions, so that call always runs GetUserPermissions and reloads the user's full permission set. The new denial cache only suppresses a repeat of the exact same user, action, name, and parent. After that reload refreshes permCache, the next Check for a different resource this user cannot access still misses the denial cache, fails the scope check, and starts another full permission query. singleflight collapses only overlapping calls for the same user and action; once that call returns, the next distinct name queries again.
