false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes are canceled when the request ends

Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection perform the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is derived with context.WithTimeoutCause from the incoming request context (Create line 51, Update line 135, Delete line 110, DeleteCollection line 163). A child context is canceled as soon as its parent is. net/http cancels the request context when ServeHTTP returns, which is immediately after these methods return the unified-storage result, so the 10s timeout never applies and Legacy.Create/Update/Delete typically fail with context.Canceled before the DB write finishes. Mode 3 exists so legacy storage stays current enough to roll back; those safety writes will systematically fail in production, and nothing retries them. The goroutines also discard the legacy error without logging, unlike the previous synchronous implementation, so the divergence is invisible aside from a metric. Detach with context.WithoutCancel (not context.Background(), which would drop user/org/trace values) before applying a timeout, and log the legacy error.

Unordered goroutines can resurrect or revert legacy objects

Every successful Create (line 50), Update (line 134), Delete (line 108), and DeleteCollection (line 161) starts an independent goroutine with no per-resource queue, generation check, or in-flight tracking. Goroutines for the same object run in parallel and can finish out of order. A create followed quickly by a delete can delete on legacy first (NotFound) and then create, resurrecting an object that unified storage has already removed. Two updates can commit the newer spec and then the older one, rolling the safety copy backward. On rollback to legacy reads, users would see deleted or stale objects. Serialize legacy writes per resource and reject a write whose unified-storage resourceVersion/generation is older than what legacy already applied.

Legacy update no longer stores the object written to unified storage

Update passes the caller's original objInfo into Legacy.Update (line 139) after Storage.Update has already applied it. The code this PR replaces loaded the unified object, computed UpdatedObject once, and passed that exact result to both stores via updateWrapper. That snapshot is required because mode 3 reads come from unified storage, so the client's resourceVersion and any patch base belong to the unified copy, not the legacy copy. Legacy.Update will call UpdatedObject again against the legacy object and enforce the unified resourceVersion, which conflicts or yields a different spec whenever the stores differ. Most updates will fail to land in legacy, so the rollback copy stops tracking writes. Write the object returned by Storage.Update into legacy instead of replaying objInfo. Create has the same shape at line 55: it forwards the pre-write input obj rather than the created object, so server-side defaults present only on the returned object are not what legacy stores.

NotFound from unified storage skips the legacy delete

Delete returns immediately on any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound (lines 101-104), and never starts the legacy delete. The previous implementation treated unified NotFound as non-fatal and still deleted from legacy. If an earlier legacy delete failed or lost the race with a later create, a client retry gets NotFound from unified storage (the source of truth) and the legacy object is left in place. After a rollback to legacy reads, that object reappears. A NotFound from unified storage should still attempt the legacy delete and ignore a legacy NotFound, since the client-facing error remains the unified result.

Destroy closes stores while legacy goroutines may still be writing

Destroy calls Storage.Destroy and Legacy.Destroy immediately and does not track the goroutines started by Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Apiserver shutdown can destroy legacy storage while those goroutines are still inside Legacy.Create/Update/Delete, which can panic on a closed backend or leave a half-applied safety write. Track in-flight legacy writes with a WaitGroup and wait for them in Destroy before tearing the stores down.

Unit tests never observe the async legacy write

TestMode3_Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection set legacy mock expectations but return as soon as the unified-storage call returns (Create at line 65). They never wait for the goroutine, never call AssertExpectations, and never check that legacy was invoked with the persisted object. Both mocks share one testify Mock, so the two Create expectations are interchangeable and a test passes even if the legacy call is skipped. They also use context.Background(), which is never canceled, so they cannot catch request-context cancellation. Inject a synchronous executor or wait for the goroutine, assert the legacy call and its arguments, and add a case whose parent context is already canceled.

Mode 3 playlist tests assume legacy is updated before the handler returns

The new mode 3 cases (file storage at line 133 and unified storage at line 192) call doPlaylistTests, which immediately lists and gets via the legacy /api/playlists endpoint after k8s create, update, and delete. Modes 0-2 mirror those writes synchronously, which is why that comparison works; mode 3 mirrors them only after the handler returns. The legacy read can therefore observe a missing or stale playlist and fail or flake, especially once the request context cancels the legacy write. If that endpoint no longer reads legacy storage, the new cases never check that the safety write landed at all. Wait until the legacy write is visible, or assert it through a hook, before comparing the two APIs.

That count matches the current bugs (Delete and Pause omitted, Silence not required to open a drawer) and will fail a fix that shows the missing actions, so CI freezes the incomplete menu. Shard splitting interpolates every query twice

runSplitQuery now always maps targets through datasource.applyTemplateVariables before grouping and execution. runShardSplitQuery does the same (shardQuerySplitting.ts:52) and then, for every shard group, calls runSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163) with targets that are already interpolated and rewritten by interpolateShardingSelector. Substitution therefore runs twice on every shard-split query. The updated shard test locks this in by expecting applyTemplateVariables 5 times for one target (once up front, once per group) and stubs an idempotent string replace, so it never fails.

applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent: it both expands variables and injects request.filters into the LogQL. The second call sees the already substituted text plus the __stream_shard__ selector. Ad hoc filters are applied again onto a selector that was not the input the injector first rewrote, so matchers are duplicated and can be attached in the wrong place, producing invalid LogQL or a selector that no longer matches the shard values fetched on the first pass. The same query with shard splitting off is interpolated only once, so shard splitting silently returns different streams. Shard path no longer pre-expands $__range, so those queries are not time-split

runShardSplitQuery used to call interpolateVariablesInQueries(request.targets, request.scopedVars), which substitutes every scoped variable, including $__range, $__range_s, and $__range_ms, against the original request range. It now calls applyTemplateVariables, which deliberately strips __range, __range_s, __range_ms, __interval, and __interval_ms out of scoped vars so those macros stay in the expression for the backend.

Previously the macro was already a constant full-range duration, the guard did not match, and the query was still chunked with a correct lookback. The previous shard entry point interpolated first and then dropped targets with a falsy expr. The new code filters on query.expr and !query.hide and only then calls applyTemplateVariables, with no second filter. A target whose expression is only a template variable that resolves to an empty string (a common optional dashboard variable) used to be removed and not executed. It is now passed into splitQueriesByStreamShard and groupTargetsByQueryType, which calls getSelectorForShardValues on that empty expression and languageProvider.fetchLabelValues for __stream_shard__. runSplitQuery later drops empty expressions, so the target is not queried, but the label lookup still runs and failures are only logged. If selector extraction throws, groupTargetsByQueryType rejects and the .then at shardQuerySplitting.ts:213 has no .catch, so the query observable never emits or completes and the panel hangs. Filter again after applyTemplateVariables, as the old interpolate-then-filter order did.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check races with the insert

When deviceLimit > 0, CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active rows for the last 30 days in one session and, if count < deviceLimit, performs INSERT ... ON CONFLICT in a second WithDbSession. There is no shared transaction, row lock, or conditional insert, so the cap is not atomic. Concurrent new devices — many browsers opening a shared anonymous dashboard, or every instance's cold cache after a restart — can all observe a count under the limit and all insert. The extra rows stay inside the 30-day window and can keep refreshing through updateDevice, so the overshoot persists until those devices age out or are deleted on login. Nothing later reconciles the table back down to the configured limit. The count and the write need to be one atomic operation that inserts only when this device_id already exists or the active count is still below the limit.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race: concurrent requests can pass the count check and insert devices beyond the limit, so the check and insert need to be atomic (transaction or lock).

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit denials are cached as successful tags

tagDeviceUI stores the device key (anon-device:<deviceID>) with SetDefault before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns, and a cache hit returns nil without touching the database. The default TTL is 29 minutes and the cache is process-local. This PR only rejects anonymous access when TagDevice returns anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached, so the first over-limit request for a new device is denied and leaves that key cached; every later request within the TTL skips the limit check, is not inserted or counted, and still receives an anonymous identity. Any other tagging error (count/insert failure, context cancel) is treated as non-fatal by Authenticate, but the poisoned key turns the following attempts into successes, so one transient database error also disables enforcement for 29 minutes. After expiry a single request fails and access is allowed again. The configured cap therefore does not limit anonymous sessions. Cache only after a successful write, and a cached denial must keep returning ErrDeviceLimitReached rather than nil.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: the cache is set before CreateOrUpdateDevice runs, so after ErrDeviceLimitReached the cached entry lets later requests skip the limit for 29 minutes.

false_positives.candidate:
Device limit is skipped when the client omits the device header

Anonymous.Authenticate denies access only when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. TagDevice returns nil without consulting deviceLimit when X-Grafana-Device-Id is missing, and again when network.GetIPFromAddress fails (invalid RemoteAddr or forwarded address). Those requests are not counted and still get a full anonymous identity with the configured anonymous org role. The header is optional and client-supplied; nothing in this path mints a server-side device id, and Anonymous.Test always returns true, so any unauthenticated request can use this client. A script, API client, or browser that omits the header — including one that was just denied and retries without it — bypasses the cap entirely, while UI clients that send the header are restricted. If device_limit is meant to restrict anonymous access, it has to run on every anonymous authentication, not only on requests that opt into device tagging.

Wire provider signatures changed without updating generated injectors

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService no longer takes anonstore.AnonStore; it now takes db.DB and builds the store internally with cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit. ProvideAnonDBStore gained a bare int64 device-limit argument. Both are Google Wire providers. The previous signature required Wire to supply an AnonStore and pass it into ProvideAnonymousDeviceService, which is what pkg/server/wire_gen.go still does — that file is not in this diff. Those generated calls will not compile. Regenerating Wire is not enough while ProvideAnonDBStore remains in the provider set, because Wire cannot inject an unnamed int64. Remove ProvideAnonDBStore from the set (the store is already constructed inside ProvideAnonymousDeviceService) and regenerate wire_gen.go before merge.

Anonymous sign-in now blocks on device tagging

TagDevice previously ran in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout, so a slow anon_device write could not delay authentication. Authenticate now calls it synchronously on the request context before returning an identity, including when AnonymousDeviceLimit is 0 (the default), where the new limit branch is skipped and the call is only an upsert. The 29-minute per-process cache hides this in steady state, but a restart or deploy clears the cache and every anonymous request then waits on the database during sign-in. With a limit configured, each of those requests also runs COUNT(*) over the 30-day window before the user is admitted. A slow anon_device table, or row locks from DeleteDevicesOlderThan, now stalls anonymous page loads and API calls instead of a background goroutine. Do the synchronous round-trip only when a configured limit must allow or deny the request.

Device-limit test never checks existing devices or auth enforcement

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit inserts one row under the limit and asserts that a second new device id is rejected by the store. It never checks that a device already inside the 30-day window can still be updated once count >= deviceLimit, which is the updateDevice path existing anonymous users depend on. A bad WHERE clause or a RowsAffected == 0 false negative would lock out every anonymous user at the cap and this test would still pass. It also never calls TagDevice or Anonymous.Authenticate, so the local-cache short-circuit, a missing X-Grafana-Device-Id, and the new auth denial are all untested. The test stays green even if every retry is granted anonymous access. Cover existing-device refresh at the cap, repeated denial for a new device through TagDevice, and Authenticate both with and without the device header.

auth.anonymous device_limit is parsed in readAuthSettings but not added to conf/defaults.ini or the configure-grafana docs. MustInt64(0) means enforcement is off, because the store only checks the cap when deviceLimit > 0; a negative or unparseable value also becomes unlimited, with no startup error. The cap counts devices whose updated_at is inside a hardcoded 30-day window, not the 61-day cleanup retention. Operators cannot discover the key, can set 0 expecting to allow no devices and instead disable the control, and cannot tell which devices consume a slot. Add the key to conf/defaults.ini with that default and document the 30-day active-device window and the 0/negative = disabled behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback bundles are not loaded on the translation path

I18n::Backend::Fallbacks resolves SiteSetting.default_locale and :en inside the backend, but the on-demand loader only runs for the active locale. I18n.translate (line 68) calls load_locale(config.locale) and never consults I18n.fallbacks, and backend fallback lookups do not go back through I18n.translate, so those YAML files stay unloaded. The new ensure_loaded! helper is only called from ApplicationController#set_locale. Mailers, jobs, rake tasks, console use, and I18n.with_locale / I18n.t(locale:) that never hit that filter therefore miss fallback strings and return a missing-translation result even when the site locale or English has the key. Argument-less lookups then store that failure in the process-wide LRU (line 74). Hot keys are not evicted, so one early lookup permanently poisons later requests in the same process even after ensure_loaded! has loaded the files.

Translation cache key ignores dynamic fallback locale

FallbackLocaleList#[] re-reads SiteSetting.default_locale on every lookup so the fallback language can change without a restart, but the accelerator cache key is only "#{key}#{config.locale}#{backend.object_id}". Nothing clears @cache when the site locale changes. Argument-less I18n.t results — including strings taken from the previous default locale and cached missing-translation placeholders — remain in the 300-entry LRU, and frequently used keys are never evicted. Fallbacks are now installed in every environment (previously only production/profile), so tests that expected a missing non-English key to raise or return a missing-translation string will silently get English instead, and the job/mailer load gap and stale-cache-after-default-locale-change bugs above would not be caught. A controller example and a non-request I18n.t (after setting a non-English locale whose fallback files are not yet loaded) need to assert both the fallback order and that a miss is not cached before the fallback bundles are loaded.

false_positives.candidate:
Imports lose embed_category unless the URL host matches

TopicEmbed.import used to pass SiteSetting.embed_category into PostCreator for every imported topic. It now passes only EmbeddableHost.record_for_host(url).try(:category_id). When that lookup returns nil or false, category is nil and the new topic is filed in uncategorized. The migration deletes the embed_category site setting and only copies it onto embeddable_hosts rows, so there is no remaining default. Feed polling (Jobs::PollFeed, triggered from TopicRetriever when feed_polling_enabled) imports article URLs that were never required to be iframe allowlist hosts. Sites that set embed_category for RSS/Atom embedding but had a blank embeddable_hosts list lose the category entirely, and any feed item whose host does not exactly match an EmbeddableHost row is created uncategorized. Existing topics are not moved; all future imports are.

Host regex rejects real hostnames the old setting allowed

validates_format_of requires a dotted hostname whose final label is [a-z]{2,5} and whose labels are separated by a single hyphen or dot. That rejects localhost, IP addresses, and any TLD longer than five characters (.museum, .photography, .international, and other gTLDs already in use), plus punycode labels that contain '--' (xn--…). The previous embeddable_hosts site setting was a free-form list and allowed those hosts. Admins cannot save them now, so embedding cannot be enabled for those origins. The optional path group in the regex is also unreachable because before_validation strips the path first.

category_id is not checked and has no foreign key

save_host writes whatever category_id is posted, and the migration declares category_id integer null: false with no foreign key or index. A deleted, unknown, or non-numeric id is stored. Category#destroy is not wired to embeddable_hosts, so deleting a category leaves dangling ids. TopicEmbed.import then passes that id to PostCreator, which cannot find the category, and new embedded topics land in uncategorized while the admin UI still shows the host as assigned. belongs_to :category does not validate existence.

Hosts are not unique, so category lookup is arbitrary

embeddable_hosts.host has no unique index, and EmbeddableHost has no uniqueness validation (case-insensitive or otherwise). After normalization, http://example.com and example.com become the same string and both can be saved, with different category_ids. record_for_host uses where(...).first with no ORDER BY, so topic import and the allow check pick an arbitrary row. Two admins, a retried migration (the INSERT is not idempotent), or duplicate lines in the old setting produce conflicting category assignments for one origin.

Plural id hydration throws and drops unresolved ids

The new _ids branch in _hydrateEmbedded calls obj[k].map with no check that the value is an array, then always deletes the original key and assigns pluralize(subType), even when _lookupSubType returns undefined. This runs for every payload with __rest_serializer == "1", not only embedding. A null or non-array *_ids attribute throws during store.find/findAll and fails the load. Id lists that are not sideloaded under the naive plural (thing + "s") are replaced with an array of undefined entries and the original ids are discarded. The previous code only rewrote singular _id keys, and only when a match was found.

New admin endpoints and the migration are untested

Admin::EmbeddableHostsController and Admin::EmbeddingController specs only assert the class ancestry. They never POST/PUT/DELETE, so a missing id 500, a nil host, invalid category_id, and the uncategorized fallback are not exercised. There is no migration spec, so the empty embed_category crash and the un-normalized host INSERT would not be caught. EmbeddableHost.host_allowed? examples use only lowercase hosts and do not cover mixed-case referers, ports, or scheme-prefixed values of the kind the old site setting accepted.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Page count is one too high when size is a multiple of the page size

totalPages uses Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. When user_count is an exact multiple of limit (including exactly 50, the default page size) that yields an extra page: 50 members render as 1/2, 100 as 3 pages, and so on. showingLast compares currentPage to that inflated total, so Next stays enabled on the last real page. next() then sets offset to user_count, findMembers returns an empty slice, and the admin sees a blank extra page of members.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug. When the member count is an exact multiple of the limit, the next action moves the offset to user_count, producing an empty last page (e.g., 2/2 with no members). The candidate also attributes this to the totalPages calculation, but the resulting empty page is the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Public group members page is silently capped at 50

Group.findMembers always requests limit 50 (the model default) and offset 0, and the public group members route only calls findMembers() with no pager. group/members.hbs iterates members and has no next/previous controls (those exist only on the admin group screen). GroupsController#members now applies that limit to every group and no longer returns the full list: non-automatic groups previously returned every member, and automatic groups defaulted to 200. Any group with more than 50 members now shows only the first page, with no indication the list is incomplete and no way to see the rest.

Creating a group ignores the selected alias level

create sets name and visible but never assigns alias_level, while update in the same controller does (params[:alias_level].to_i when present). The admin form shows the alias-level combo box for new groups (it is outside the {{#if id}} block), and Group.asJSON sends alias_level on POST /admin/groups. The chosen level is discarded and the row keeps the default (0 / nobody). The client model still holds the unsaved value, so the dropdown looks correct until reload, when it reverts. The create spec only checks name stripping, so this is untested.

Update forces visible to false when the param is omitted

update sets group.visible = params[:visible] == "true" unconditionally, unlike alias_level and name which are applied only when present. Any PUT or PATCH that does not include visible=true therefore hides the group and still returns 200. resources :groups still routes PATCH to update, and the removed update_patch path used to change membership without touching visible. A leftover PATCH {changes: {add: ...}} (old admin JS or an API client) now adds nobody and silently sets visible to false. Partial updates that only rename the group do the same.

Adding members does not trim names and can commit a partial update

add_members splits usernames on commas and looks each piece up with User.find_by_username without stripping. A normal typed value such as "alice, bob" looks up " bob", matches nobody, and is skipped. Unknown names are ignored and the action still returns success, so the admin UI reloads an unchanged list and cannot tell the user who was not added. group.add on an already-persisted group inserts the join row immediately, and the loop is not wrapped in a transaction: if a later name raises (duplicate membership / RecordNotUnique), earlier adds stay committed while the request 500s. The new spec only posts already-clean comma-separated names, so none of this is covered.

Member removal bypasses Group#remove and 404s if already gone

remove_member calls group.users.delete(user_id) instead of Group#remove, which the previous membership path used. Passing an id makes ActiveRecord find the user inside the association first, so a user who is not currently a member raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound (404) rather than succeeding as a no-op. For a has_many :through with no :dependent option, delete then delete_alls join rows and skips GroupUser destroy callbacks. Adds go through group.add, which is what keeps user_count in sync (the index spec expects user_count == 1 after add). Removals can therefore leave user_count, titles, or primary-group side effects stale. The new spec only asserts users.count after a successful delete, so that drift would still pass. The admin client also has no error handler on this request, so a 404 leaves the member on screen with no message.

Members endpoint does not bound limit or offset

limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i and offset = params[:offset].to_i are passed straight into the query. There is no maximum, so anyone who can see a group (including anonymous users, for a visible automatic group such as trust_level_0) can pass limit=1000000 and force the process to load and serialize the entire membership. Negative values are also accepted: PostgreSQL rejects LIMIT -1 and OFFSET -1, so a request like limit=-1 returns 500. A zero limit is echoed back to the admin client, which then divides by zero in totalPages and renders a broken pager.

Out-of-range member offsets are echoed back as a blank page

offset is taken from params with to_i and returned unchanged in meta.offset, even when it is past the end of the list. After the admin removes the last member on a page, Group.removeMember calls findMembers without moving offset backward. The client clamp uses the pre-request user_count (still the old total), so it still requests the old offset. The server, now with fewer users, returns an empty members array and the same offset; the client stores that offset. The UI sits on a blank page (and, with the off-by-one page count, may show 2/2 for a list that now fits on one page) until the admin clicks Previous. Negative offsets are likewise not corrected and make PostgreSQL raise.

Enter in the group form activates Add instead of Save

The new form wraps the name field, the user selector, and the action buttons, but none of the buttons set type="button" and the form has no submit handler. In HTML the default button type is submit, and pressing Enter in a text field synthetically clicks the first submit button in the form. Once the group has an id, that button is Add, not Save. Enter in the name field therefore runs addMembers (re-adding whatever is still in the username box) and does not save the name, visibility, or alias level. If Ember's action helper does not preventDefault, the form also does a GET navigation of the current admin URL and discards the in-page state. On a new group the first button is Save, so Enter behaves differently before and after the first save.

Add and remove failures are silent and the username field is never cleared

addMembers posts the usernames and, on success, does not clear the field (the TODO on the previous line). removeMember and addMembers both ignore rejected promises. A 422 (automatic group), 404 (member already gone), 500 (duplicate add), or network error closes the confirm dialog or clicks Add and then changes nothing on screen, so the admin cannot tell failure from a no-op. Because the field stays filled, a second click resubmits the same names; if Group#add raises on a duplicate, that second click 500s. Newly added users are also only reloaded on the current offset, so someone who sorts onto another page never appears in the list even though the request succeeded.

Username box is not reset when switching groups

Admin group controllers are Ember singletons. setupController replaces the model and reloads members but does not clear controller.usernames. The add-members field is bound to that controller property, and addMembers never clears it after a successful add either. Navigating from group A to group B leaves A's pending (or just-added) usernames in the box; clicking Add then PUTs those names onto group B. Offset is stored on the group model so it does not leak, but usernames were left on the shared controller when membership was split out of the save payload.

Member reloads use the unsaved name from the text field

findMembers builds GET /groups/<name>/members.json from this.get('name'), and the admin name input is two-way bound to that property. Editing the name and then paging, adding, or removing a member fetches (or fails to fetch) the unsaved name before Save. Remove itself uses the numeric id and can succeed, but the follow-up findMembers 404s, so the list never refreshes and the removed user stays on screen. The name is also interpolated without encodeURIComponent, so a value that still contains spaces produces a broken URL. Pagination has already written the new offset before the request, so a failed reload leaves the page indicator and the member list out of sync.

Client keeps the unstripped name after create

create() only copies resp.basic_group.id from the POST response. The server strips the name before save and returns the stored name on BasicGroupSerializer, but the in-memory group keeps whatever was typed, including leading or trailing spaces. showGroup then navigates with that unsaved name, so a refresh looks the group up by the spaced name, misses the record named "bob", and the admin route sends the user back to the index. A later Save sends the spaced name to update, which assigns params[:name] with no strip (create strips, update does not). That either fails name-format validation or writes the spaces back over the cleaned name.

GET group members no longer returns a bare array

GroupsController#members used to render_serialized an array of GroupUserSerializer objects. It now returns {members, meta: {total, limit, offset}}. The in-repo Group.findMembers client was updated, but any other caller — plugins, API scripts, or a browser still running the previous JS that did result.map(...) — will throw because the top-level JSON is an object. The reverse is also true during a rolling deploy: new JS expects result.members and result.meta and crashes on the old array. There is no versioned path or compatibility shim, and no spec locks the new contract.

Overlapping member-page requests can land on the wrong page

next and previous write offset and call findMembers immediately, and the pager links are not disabled while a request is in flight. Two quick clicks start two GETs; findMembers applies whichever response arrives last via setProperties, including that response's offset. A slower response for the previous page overwrites a later click, so the list and the page indicator show a page the admin already left. Nothing ignores a stale response.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? writes during validation and double-counts

should_block? is not a pure predicate: on every hit it does match_count += 1, sets last_match_at, and calls record.save, and EmailValidator calls it from User validation. UsersController#create always evaluates user.valid? and then user.save, and save runs validations again, so one signup attempt invokes should_block? twice. The first save commits immediately. The second runs inside the user-save transaction: if the user is persisted (including action_type do_nothing, which still updates stats), both increments commit and match_count rises by 2; if validation fails, the inner increment rolls back and the count rises by 1. Paths that only save once, such as User.create_for_email, rise by 1. Any valid? call, including a check that never creates a user, also mutates the row. The read-modify-write is racy under concurrent signups, and a failure in that save (lock timeout, StatementInvalid) escapes the validator and is rescued in create as login.something_already_taken. Record the match with one atomic UPDATE that does not run validations, and do not write from inside validation on every valid?/save pass.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate makes the same point as the golden comment. The predicate updates match statistics as a side effect during a check, and that read-modify-write is racy under concurrent signups. The candidate adds extra detail on double-counting.

true_positives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Domain allow/deny regex is unanchored and can be bypassed

email_in_restriction_setting? builds Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true) after only escaping dots, then uses value =~ regexp, which succeeds on any substring. With email_domains_whitelist set to example.com, attacker@example.com.evil.com matches @example.com and is treated as allowed. Someone who controls that domain can receive the activation message and register even though the address is not on example.com. The same pattern does not cover subdomains on the blacklist: spam.com does not match user@mail.spam.com, so a subdomain of a blocked provider is accepted. Other metacharacters in the site setting are interpolated raw, so a value with an unmatched parenthesis makes Regexp.new raise and turns every email change into a 500. Compare normalized domains (anchor at the end of the address, or split the setting and test equality) instead of a substring regex.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same flaw: the @(#{domains}) regex in email_in_restriction_setting? has no proper boundary anchoring, so the whitelist can be bypassed. The candidate gives a different bypass example (example.com.evil.com) than the golden comment's suffix/subdomain example, but the root cause and the fix (anchor or compare domains exactly) are the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocklist lookup is case-sensitive and does not trim

BlockedEmail.should_block? loads a row with BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first, and the model never normalizes email before the uniqueness check or save. Signup stores the address exactly as submitted (User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] with no downcase or strip), and the new client cache compares that same raw string via rejectedEmails.contains. On PostgreSQL the unique index and equality match are case-sensitive, so a block row for bad@spam.com does not match Bad@spam.com, BAD@spam.com, or bad@spam.com with leading or trailing whitespace. Those are the same mailbox in practice (UsersController#change_email already does Email.downcase(...).strip), so a blocked address can still register by changing case or padding spaces, and after one rejection the signup form will allow that variant through again. Downcase and strip on write and inside should_block? before the query, and enforce case-insensitive uniqueness so mixed-case duplicates cannot be stored.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same problem: the email lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? is case-sensitive, so a mixed-case variant can bypass the block. It adds whitespace trimming, but the core bug is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Email change never consults the blocklist

The new block check only runs from EmailValidator when a User is validated with email_changed?. UsersController#change_email never assigns user.email or saves the user. It only rejects the address if User.where("email = ?", lower_email).exists?, then creates an EmailToken and enqueues an authorization mail to that address. A blocked address therefore passes this endpoint and a confirmation message is sent. true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

`i.content.scrub` assumes every item has a string `content` and that `String#scrub` exists. Standard RSS 2.0 only has `description` (SimpleRSS sets `content` from `content:encoded`), so `i.content` is nil and this raises NoMethodError on the first such item. `String#scrub` itself was added in Ruby 2.1, so on Ruby 2.0/1.9 the call fails even when content is present. There is no per-item rescue, and `sidekiq_options retry: false`, so one bad item aborts the rest of the feed until the next hour. `TopicRetriever` calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute` inline before the HTTP fallback, so the same exception also skips `import_remote` for the URL the user actually asked to embed. `feed_key` is computed and never used, and `open` is not given a timeout or closed.

The extra concerns it raises (Ruby version, retries, unused `feed_key`, missing timeout) do not change that the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
import_remote fetches the embed URL with open-uri and follows redirects

`import_remote` does `open(url).read` with no `require 'open-uri'` in this file (only `poll_feed.rb` requires it), no read size limit, no timeout, and no close. Unless some other file has already loaded open-uri, `Kernel#open` treats the URL as a local path and raises Errno::ENOENT, so the non-RSS embed path never imports. When open-uri is loaded, it follows HTTP redirects. `TopicRetriever` only compares the original URL's host to `embeddable_host`, so `http://allowed-host/redirect` that 302s to `http://127.0.0.1`, link-local cloud metadata, or another internal service is fetched and then stored as a public topic via the raw_html path. The embed action enqueues that fetch for any client that can set `Referer` to the allowed host. The same method is also called from the Disqus importer with links taken from the XML, with no host allowlist. Failures are unrescued, so a 404, SSL error, or huge body fails the job.

embed_url is varchar(255) under a unique index

`t.string :embed_url` is a varchar(255) on PostgreSQL, and the unique index is on that column. Article URLs with long slugs or tracking query strings routinely exceed 255 characters. `TopicEmbed.create!` then raises a string-right-truncation error, the import transaction rolls back, and that article can never be embedded. The column needs to be `text` (or a much larger limit); a unique btree index on text is valid in PostgreSQL.

Disqus import drops threads when the live page cannot be fetched

Topic creation used to be a local `PostCreator` call with the export title, `created_at`, permalink body, and optional `-c` category. It now depends entirely on `TopicEmbed.import_remote`, which GETs `t[:link]` and returns nil on any network, HTTP, or readability failure. The comment loop is inside `if post.present?`, so a dead or blocked link silently skips every comment on that thread. `import_remote` / `TopicEmbed.import` also have no `created_at` or category argument, and the `-c` / `--category` option was removed, so existing invocations that passed a category fail and imported topics are dated now in the default category instead of the original thread date and destination.

`skip_validations: true` only turns off ActiveRecord validations. `Post` still includes `RateLimiter::OnCreateRecord` (`rate_limit` / `rate_limit_create_post`, plus topic creation limits in `TopicCreator`), and those callbacks run on save. A feed or retrieve that creates more than a handful of topics in one run will raise `RateLimiter::LimitExceeded` or roll back mid-loop; `PollFeed` has no per-item rescue, so the rest of the feed is skipped until the limit window resets (`max_topics_per_day` is 20). The Disqus task in this same change calls `RateLimiter.disable` around its import loop; `PollFeed` and `TopicRetriever` do not. Updates pass `bypass_rate_limiter`, but that flag only skips `EditRateLimiter` inside `PostRevisor`, not create limits.

Every embed miss re-downloads and imports the entire feed

When `feed_polling_enabled?` is set, each cache miss calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute` synchronously inside the retrieve job, before the single-URL HTTP fetch. The Redis throttle key is per embed URL, not per feed, so ten different articles trigger ten full feed downloads and imports per minute, on top of the hourly schedule (this path does not take the scheduler lock, so it can overlap the hourly run). `PollFeed#feed_key` looks like a conditional-GET / already-seen short-circuit but is never read, and `poll_feed` always `open`s the feed URL and walks every item. One slow or huge feed blocks the worker and can create a topic for every item as a side effect of viewing a single embed.

Retrieve throttle can stick forever if expire does not run

`retrieved_recently?` does `SETNX retrieved:<url> 1` and only then `EXPIRE 60`. Those are not atomic. If the process dies, Redis errors, or expire is skipped between the two calls, the key has no TTL. `retrieved_recently?` then stays true for that exact URL forever (unless `no_throttle` is set for staff), so the article is never fetched again. Use a single `SET key 1 NX EX 60` (or set the TTL inside the same command the deployment's Redis supports). The same gap exists for every distinct embed URL.

Embed URLs are compared exactly, so the same article splits or is skipped

Lookup, uniqueness, and the import short-circuit all use the raw URL string (`where(embed_url: url)` and the unique index). There is no normalization: `http://host/a` and `http://host/a/`, a URL with a fragment or `utm_*` query, and the same path with a different scheme case are different rows, so one article becomes multiple topics. The allowlist check is also case-sensitive: `TopicRetriever#invalid_host?` uses `URI(embed_url).host`, which preserves case (`Example.COM`), and compares it to `SiteSetting.embeddable_host` with `!=`. `TopicEmbed.import` only accepts URLs matching `/^https?:\/\//`, so `HTTP://...` is dropped. `EmbedController#ensure_embeddable` uses the same case-sensitive host compare on `Referer`. `belongs_to :topic` / `:post` do not declare `dependent: :destroy`, and `Topic` is not given a matching association, so destroying a topic or its first post leaves `topic_embeds` in place (there is also no foreign key). The embed action then does `TopicView.new(topic_id, ...)` for a missing topic and 500s on every view instead of importing again. On the next feed change, `post = embed.post` is nil and `PostRevisor.new(post)` raises, which aborts the rest of `PollFeed`'s item loop. `import` also treats any in-memory `PostCreator` result as success (`post.present?` is true for an unsaved post after a rolled-back create) and will `create!` an embed pointing at a topic id that was never committed.

`ensure_embeddable` only compares `Referer`'s host to `embeddable_host`. That header is not a credential; any client can send `Referer: http://<embeddable_host>/` and GET `/embed/best?embed_url=...`. The helper claims to absolutize relative URLs but only rewrites `a[href]` and `img[src]` that `start_with?('/')`. A protocol-relative URL such as `//cdn.example.com/a.png` matches that check, then `sub(/^\/+/, '')` strips both slashes, so it is rewritten to `http://<article-host>/cdn.example.com/a.png` instead of keeping the CDN host. Both forms are common in RSS and article HTML. Only root-relative paths like `/hello` work, which is the only case the new spec covers.

`contents << footer` appends to the caller's string instead of copying it. `import_remote` passes `doc.content` through, and Readability returns nil when it cannot extract an article, so this raises NoMethodError and the retrieve job fails (the loading iframe then retries forever). A frozen string raises the same way. Callers that reuse the buffer also get a second footer and a different SHA1 on the next import. Build a new string (`"#{contents}#{footer}"`) after rejecting blank content.

The success examples do not call `render_views` (rspec-rails 2 stubs views by default), so they never compile `best.html.erb` and cannot catch the `end if` syntax error. The example that expects a topic view stubs `TopicView.new` without a return value; mocha yields nil, so `@topic_view` is nil and a real render would raise before the `after` hook's `response.should be_success`. `spec/jobs/poll_feed_spec.rb` only stubs whether `execute` calls `poll_feed` and never parses a feed, so the nil-`content` crash and unsanitized import are also untested.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

If there is no row, tu is nil and this raises NoMethodError, so the request 500s and nothing is saved. A topic_users row is not created for every user who can see a topic; the URL is predictable and any logged-in user who can see the topic can open it without having visited or been emailed. false_positives.candidate:
Unsubscribe is a state-changing GET

TopicsController#unsubscribe is exposed as GET t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe and t/:topic_id/unsubscribe, and it writes topic_users.notification_level before rendering. Rails CSRF protection does not cover GET, and this app predates SameSite cookies, so a logged-in victim can be forced to change topic or PM notification level by an image, link prefetch, or other cross-site GET. The write is also not idempotent: a level above regular becomes regular, and regular becomes muted, so a refresh or a second full page load applies a second transition (watching becomes regular, then muted). The Ember unsubscribe route never performs the change itself, so the only implementation of the action is this GET side effect.

Unsubscribe leaves tracking and watching users notified

The email string says the link will stop notifications for this topic, and the new page says the user will stop receiving them, but unsubscribe only sets notification_level to muted when it is already regular (1) or lower. Tracking (2) and watching (3) are both written to regular (1). Tracking receives the same reply, mention, and quote emails as regular, so that click changes nothing about email. Watching stops every-post emails but still sends reply, mention, and quote emails. A second request then takes regular to muted, so the first confirmation is false and a refresh changes the result.

Raw save does not record an explicit notification choice

unsubscribe assigns notification_level and calls save! instead of TopicUser.change. change is what sets notifications_changed_at, sets notifications_reason_id to user_changed, and publishes the /topic/:id notification_level_change event. save! leaves the old reason in place. Rows created when an email is sent often have a nil reason, because TopicUser.change is called with only last_emailed_post_number. update_last_read in topic_user.rb then forces notification_level back to tracking when notifications_reason_id is null and the auto-track time threshold is met, and auto_track does the same for a nil reason. For those users the unsubscribe does not stick, and already-open clients never get the level-change event.

Unsubscribe template does not match its route

The router registers a top-level topicUnsubscribe route at /t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe, and the route, controller, and view are all the topic-unsubscribe module. Ember looks up template topic-unsubscribe, i.e. templates/topic-unsubscribe. The template was added at templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs, which is the name for a nested topic.unsubscribe route that was not registered, and there is no matching topic/unsubscribe controller. After the Rails shell boots, the transition fails with a missing template, so the confirmation text and the notification dropdown never render.

Per-topic unsubscribe link is not tied to the recipient

Topic#unsubscribe_url is only the public topic URL plus /unsubscribe, and UserNotifications puts that same link in every recipient's mail. TopicsController#unsubscribe is behind ensure_logged_in and always updates current_user, with no signed user or email token. Unlike the existing digest path email/unsubscribe/:key, a logged-out recipient opening the message from a mail client is not unsubscribed by the click. If someone else is logged in (forwarded mail or a shared browser), that account's notification level is changed instead of the recipient's.

render :show drops canonical URL on topic pages

perform_show_response is also used by TopicsController#show, which calls canonical_url only after perform_show_response returns. Previously the HTML format block did not render, so Rails deferred the template until the action finished and @canonical_url was already set for the layout. The new render :show inside format.html renders the layout immediately, before that call, so every topic HTML response loses its canonical link. Unsubscribe HTML has the same gap because it never sets a canonical URL either.

No coverage of unsubscribe behavior or the new link

The only spec change passes unsubscribe_url into Email::MessageBuilder so the new unsubscribe_link translation does not raise MissingInterpolationArgument, but the example still only checks that the user-preferences URL appears in the text body. It never asserts that the per-topic unsubscribe URL is present in the text or HTML part, or that List-Unsubscribe changed. There is no controller or request spec for TopicsController#unsubscribe, so the level transition, nil TopicUser crash, slug redirect, and session requirements are untested.

A fully blocked date is stored as an override whose start and end are the same instant, and this function tries to treat that as unavailable for the whole day. The check is dayjs(...) === dayjs(...). Those are two different objects, so reference equality is never true, even when both instants match. The later before/after checks then only exclude slots that do not overlap that single point, leaving a bookable hole around the shifted timestamp. For a UTC−5 host blocked at 00:00, the instant is shifted to 05:00Z, and a slot that overlaps 05:00Z is reported available on a day the host marked unavailable. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug: two dayjs objects are compared with ===, which checks object references and so never returns true. Both recommend using isSame instead.

That return is before the busy-interval loop, so Google Calendar conflicts and existing Cal.com bookings are never consulted. isFixed is true for every user when schedulingType is null and for every collective host, and the same helper is used for fixed and round-robin hosts, so this is not limited to the round-robin case. On any day that has a date override, the public schedule can offer times when that host is already busy, which is what the booking page presents.

Multiple override windows on one day remove all slots

The new override scan uses dateOverrides.find and treats a truthy callback as "this slot is unavailable". The callback returns true when the slot is entirely before or entirely after that one window, and find stops at the first such window. A normal split override (for example 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00 on the same date) therefore rejects every slot, because every slot lies outside at least one window, and the day shows no availability. The predicate is also too weak in the other direction: it only excludes slots that end at or before the window start or start after the window end, so a slot that starts before the window and ends inside it is treated as bookable. The left side is built with dayjs(date.start) in local mode, so format uses the Node process timezone. If that timezone is not UTC, an override whose shifted instant falls on a different local calendar date than its UTC date does not match the slot. US evening overrides, which land in the 00:00–04:00Z window, are the typical case: dateOverrideExist stays false and the override is silently ignored, so the fixed host is treated as on their normal hours. Both sides need to be formatted in UTC, or the day bounds compared as absolute instants.

Date overrides are stored as the organizer's wall-clock time encoded in a UTC timestamp (a 14:00 IST override is 14:00Z, which the existing tests rely on). The new code adds inviteeOffset − organizerOffset minutes and then keeps only .hour() and .minute(), so a result on the previous or next calendar day cannot be represented. A 20:00–23:00 organizer-UTC override viewed from UTC+3 becomes 23:00 and 02:00; end-minute 120 is less than start-minute 1380, buildSlots drops any range whose start is not before its end, and the host's normal hours for that day were already removed, so the attendee sees no slots instead of 23:00–02:00. The PR adds a destructive delete and a failure counter with no tests. Nothing asserts that an email or WhatsApp reminder with retryCount > 1 is kept, that an already scheduled SMS row is kept, that a missing phone number does not spin until the event date, or that an SMS reminder is removed only after two failures and not on the first. Those are the branches this change gets wrong, and a fixture test of the delete filter and the increment paths would have caught them.

OR SQL fragments are unsafe to AND with more predicates

Team and org authorization SQL is an OR of a team-booking predicate and a personal-booking predicate, joined as `(${left}) OR (${right})` in buildOrgAuthorizationCondition and buildTeamAuthorizationCondition. That groups each side only; it does not parenthesize the whole OR. When eventTypeId and memberUserId are absent, getBaseConditions returns that fragment unchanged. SQL binds AND tighter than OR, so a caller query `WHERE ${conditions} AND "startTime" >= ${from}` is parsed as team-booking-predicate OR (personal-booking-predicate AND startTime >= from). Every team booking for an authorized team is included even when it fails the date range or any other AND predicate the caller adds. The event-type filter has the same shape, `("eventTypeId" = id) OR ("eventParentId" = id)`, with no outer parentheses. Interpolating it as `WHERE ${auth} AND ${eventTypeFilter}` is parsed as (auth AND eventTypeId = id) OR (eventParentId = id), so any booking whose parent event type matches is returned even if authorization fails. getBaseConditions does wrap both sides when a filter is present, but the no-filter return value and the public getAuthorizationConditions/getFilterConditions fragments are not embed-safe. The old Prisma where-objects were grouped by the query engine, so this is a regression of the raw-SQL conversion. Wrap every fragment in an outer pair of parentheses before returning it.

Prisma.sql toEqual checks do not match nested fragments

The team-scope assertion here, the org-scope assertion around line 332, and the combined-filter assertion around line 429 expect a single flat Prisma.sql template via toEqual. The service builds those conditions with Array.reduce, nesting Prisma.sql fragments, and Prisma.sql does not flatten nested fragments until execution. The actual object has inner Sql values; the expected object has raw ids and arrays in values. Deep equality fails even when the SQL text and parameters match, so these tests fail in CI and do not validate authorization or filter SQL. Compare a flattened statement and parameter list, or execute the SQL.

Team and org authorization SQL is never executed

The only database query in this file is the user-scope getBaseConditions case, which is userId equality AND teamId IS NULL. Team and org authorization, including teamId/userId = ANY(array) and the isTeamBooking OR groups, are only compared as objects. PostgreSQL array binding for Prisma raw parameters and AND/OR precedence are therefore untested. Execute those fragments with $queryRaw against rows that must be included and rows that must be excluded (another org's team, a non-member personal booking, a team booking versus a personal booking, and an extra AND predicate such as a date range).

Reschedules and workflow deletes fill that cap, later cancels fail, and those emails are still sent. Failures are caught inside the helper, so the caller continues as if cancellation worked. On reschedule the booking is kept, the row is left with cancelled unset, and the cron only cancels cancelled=true rows, so it will not retry. On workflow and step deletion the POST is not awaited and the following delete cascade-removes the reminder (WorkflowStep/Workflow onDelete: Cascade). If the POST has not finished or failed because of the cap, the batch id is gone and the cron cannot retry, so the email is sent. Far-future sends should only set cancelled and keep the row. That leaves orphaned or unretried records and is inconsistent with the other path. The candidate adds further consequences, such as the SendGrid cap and cascade timing, but the core flaw is the same.

All email cancels are deferred, so reminders due before the next cron are still sent

For any reminder that already has a referenceId, cancellation only sets cancelled=true and never calls SendGrid, no matter how soon scheduledDate is. The only follow-up is the scheduleEmailReminders cron (PR: every 15 minutes), which cancels batches whose scheduledDate is within the next hour. SendGrid will not cancel a scheduled send less than 10 minutes before sendAt. If the booking is cancelled after the last cron run that is still more than 10 minutes before send time, the next run either happens after scheduledDate — and that job first deletes every EMAIL reminder with scheduledDate <= now, so cancel is never attempted — or SendGrid rejects the late cancel. The reminder is delivered. This is the common case of cancelling shortly before a reminder. Deferral also does not protect the 100-cap for sends already inside the one-hour window, because those cancellations would be pending for under an hour either way. Reminders already inside that window should be cancelled immediately; only later sends should be flagged for the cron.

Past-due reminders are deleted before SendGrid cancellation is attempted

The cron starts by deleting every EMAIL WorkflowReminder with scheduledDate <= now, including rows with cancelled=true, and only then loads reminders to cancel (lines 44-51). The row is the only copy of the SendGrid batch id. If an earlier run did not cancel that batch (downtime, a thrown cancel aborting the loop, or the booking being cancelled after the last pre-send run), SendGrid still has the scheduled mail and this delete makes a later cancel impossible. Past-due cleanup must not remove cancelled rows until a SendGrid cancel has been attempted and the outcome recorded. As written, any missed window permanently fails the fix.

One SendGrid cancel failure aborts the rest and skips DB cleanup

remindersToCancel is handled in a single try/catch. Each POST is awaited in order, and the prisma deletes are only executed after every request succeeds. Any rejection — the 100 pending-cancellation cap, SendGrid refusing a cancel inside its 10-minute cutoff, a null referenceId, or a network error — jumps to the catch, which only logs, then the handler goes on to schedule new mail. Later reminders in that run are not cancelled. Rows whose POST already succeeded are not deleted, so the next run must redo them. A row that fails every time stays in the result set until its scheduledDate passes and the earlier deleteMany removes it, and each run that hits it aborts the rest of the batch, so those other cancelled reminders are sent. The query also does not require method EMAIL or a non-null referenceId, so one bad row is enough to fail the POST. If the booking is paid, this branch refunds, sets status to REJECTED, and returns "Booking successfully cancelled." before the reminder block at line 484. That block is the only place this handler marks email reminders cancelled or deletes SMS reminders. The earlier return null when the payment app is missing (around line 437) skips it too. Paid event types can still have workflows, and bookingToDelete already loads workflowReminders, but they are ignored on this path. A cancelled paid booking therefore keeps its scheduled emails and SMS. If the reminder was not yet handed to SendGrid, the cron's unscheduled query does not check booking status and will schedule and send it; if it was already scheduled, the cron only cancels rows with cancelled=true, which was never set. Reminder cancellation has to run on this path before returning.

An existing step is treated as edited when JSON.stringify(oldStep) !== JSON.stringify(newStep). oldStep is a Prisma WorkflowStep and always includes numberVerificationPending; newStep is the zod input and has senderName instead, so the comparison is always true even when nothing changed. The branch used to delete the WorkflowReminder row; that deleteMany was removed. It now only calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder (line 576), which sets cancelled and leaves the SendGrid scheduled send in place, and that call is not awaited. The same request then scheduleEmailReminder's a new batch for every future booking of that step. Every workflow save therefore leaves the previous batches live until the cron's one-hour window and adds another set. Near-term reminders can be delivered twice. All superseded batches become pending cancellations in the same hour, which can exceed SendGrid's 100-cap and cause the cron cancel loop to fail. Compare the actual editable fields, and do not create the replacement send until the previous batch is flagged or cancelled.

No tests for deferred cancel or the cron SendGrid cancellation loop

The PR replaces SendGrid cancellation and adds a cron path, but no test covers deleteScheduledEmailReminder, the cancelled flag, reschedule/workflow-delete behavior, or the scheduleEmailReminders cancellation loop. The previous fix used the wrong SendGrid endpoint and failed in production once 100 pending cancellations accumulated. Without a test that a far-future cancel only sets cancelled, that an imminent cancel actually stops the batch, and that one failed POST does not skip the remaining rows, the same production failure can regress unnoticed.
